# Lux (Doctor Who)

## In-Universe Biography and Canonical Status

Lux Imperator is a fictional character and the titular main antagonist of the second episode of Doctor Who Series 15, titled 'Lux' . He is a transcendental entity who serves as the God of Light within a larger pantheon of antagonistic deities , , . His canonical designation is explicitly stated in dialogue within the episode, where he declares himself to be "Lux. Lux Imperator, the God of Light. I am the dazzle at the heart of the pantheon, and the glint in the eyes of the mad" , . This title establishes his identity as a being of immense power and significance within the Whoniverse's mythos. The full name "Lux Imperator" is derived from Latin, translating to "Light Emperor," further cementing his thematic association with radiance and dominion over illumination . It is crucial to distinguish this character from others in the series also named "Lux" to maintain narrative and encyclopedic accuracy . The episode makes it clear that this incarnation of Lux is not a re-use of previous characters, such as the immortal companion Ashildr, whose alias has been informally associated with the name in some contexts , .

The character made his sole canonical appearance in the single-episode installment of Series 15, which premiered on April 19, 2025 [), )]. The episode, written by showrunner Russell T Davies and directed by Amanda Brotchie, runs for approximately 43 to 45 minutes, depending on the source and broadcast platform [), , ]. Lux Imperator is voiced by actor Alan Cumming, marking his return to the series seven years after portraying King James I in the Series 11 episode 'The Witchfinders' [), ]. Cumming was personally invited to join the cast by Davies, highlighting the deliberate choice to bring his performance to the role . This singular appearance positions Lux as a newly created character introduced specifically to expand the lore surrounding the Pantheon, a recurring theme in the modern era of Doctor Who . The Pantheon itself is described with slight variations across sources, referred to interchangeably as the "Pantheon of Discord" or the "Pantheon of Chaos" [), , ]. This group consists of powerful, god-like beings whose mission is to alter reality and sow chaos; confirmed members include Lux Imperator, Sutekh (the God of Death), the Toymaker (the God of Games), and Maestro (the God of Music) , . The episode establishes that the Pantheon is fully aware of the Doctor's recent victories over its members, positioning Lux's emergence as a direct consequence of this established history of conflict [)].

The narrative of 'Lux' is set in Miami, Florida, during the year 1952, a period marked by racial segregation and Jim Crow laws [), ]. The story unfolds primarily within the Palazzo Movie Theatre, an abandoned cinema where patrons disappear nightly, only to be found trapped inside individual frames of a film strip [), ]. This setting is not merely a backdrop but an integral part of the plot, used to explore themes of historical trauma, systemic racism, and visibility , . The inclusion of a non-white lead duo, featuring Ncuti Gatwa as the Fifteenth Doctor and Varada Sethu as Belinda Chandra, was a deliberate creative choice by writer Russell T Davies to reflect a more inclusive vision of the world, aiming to make audiences feel "visible, you feel seen" . The episode uses this specific historical context to critique superficial representations of history, framing the Doctor's mission not just as a supernatural investigation but as a confrontation with real-world injustice , . Lux Imperator's arrival in this environment is tied to the cinematic medium itself, as he enters the primary universe through a unique confluence of moonlight reflecting off a spoon onto celluloid film stock during a screening , . This origin story grounds his seemingly surreal existence in the tangible technology of early cinema, reinforcing his identity as a creature of light and illusion. His presence disrupts the timeline, trapping fifteen people, including a young boy named Tommy Lee Lowenstein, by converting them into two-dimensional images on a flammable celluloid strip [), ].

This detailed canonical framework establishes Lux Imperator as a significant, albeit one-off, addition to the Doctor Who mythos. His introduction is carefully woven into the existing narrative tapestry, connecting him to past conflicts with the Pantheon while simultaneously grounding his story in a specific historical and technological context. His status as a new character, distinct from all prior incarnations named "Lux," allows the narrative to explore fresh thematic territory centered on the nature of fiction, the power of light, and the complexities of confronting historical injustice , .

## Narrative Role and Plot Function

Lux Imperator's narrative function in the Doctor Who episode 'Lux' is multifaceted, serving as both a formidable supernatural antagonist and a complex meta-fictional device , . His entry into the primary universe in 1952 Miami was contingent upon a rare cosmic alignment: moonlight had to reflect off a spoon onto a celluloid film projector, requiring a precise combination of reflection, electricity, and cinematic projection , . This methodical, almost whimsical origin underscores his fundamental nature as a being intrinsically linked to the medium of film and light . Once manifested, his primary objective became acquiring a physical, three-dimensional body—a desire that drove his entire plotline , . He accomplished this by trapping fifteen individuals, including the young Tommy Lee Lowenstein, inside separate frames of a film reel, effectively transforming them into living cartoons [), ]. This act of entrapment served a dual purpose: it provided him with a steady source of cinematic projection light to sustain his existence and allowed him to manipulate those around him to achieve his goals .

His most significant interaction within the narrative was with Reginald Pye, the film operator at the Palazzo Cinema . Lux manipulated Pye by exploiting his grief over the death of his wife, promising him visions of her if he continued to project films . This pact reveals a key aspect of Lux's character: his willingness to exploit profound human emotions for his own ends. However, this relationship also highlights a vulnerability, as Lux's own motivations are revealed to stem from a deep-seated loneliness and a simple, childlike desire—to go outside and become "a real boy" . This poignant motivation adds a layer of tragic complexity to his otherwise malevolent actions, positioning him not as a purely evil entity but as a being bound by rules and desires that are both divine and deeply personal. He is bound by the constraints of his Mr. Ring-a-Ding form, which dictates certain behaviors, such as being forced to sing his full theme song if played, and honor-bound to answer questions about his origins and methods truthfully, though he often cloaks these answers in riddles .

The central conflict of the episode revolves around the Fifteenth Doctor and his companion, Belinda Chandra, who arrive at the cinema to investigate the mass disappearances [), ]. Upon discovering the truth, the Doctor and Belinda themselves become ensnared by Lux, who traps them inside the animated dimension of the film , . Within this surreal, hand-drawn world, Lux attempts to break their spirit by forcing them to confront their deepest fears, particularly their anxieties about home and belonging . The Doctor's fear of returning to Gallifrey and Belinda's fear of never seeing her family again manifest physically within the cartoon realm, adding emotional weight to the abstract battle . Lux's ultimate plan was to absorb the Doctor's remaining regeneration energy, which would grant him true corporeality and allow him to transcend his two-dimensional existence , . This ambition places him directly in opposition to the Doctor, whom he identifies as "Enemy of the Toymaker, decomposer of Maestro, the killer of the god of death," acknowledging the Doctor's prior victories over other members of the Pantheon . This establishes a direct line of continuity and escalating threat, making Lux a logical successor to previous Pantheon adversaries.

The climax of the narrative sees Lux's plans unravel due to the clever agency of Belinda Chandra and the assistance of Reginald Pye . When Lux absorbs the Doctor's regeneration energy, he momentarily achieves a grotesque, hyper-detailed three-dimensional form before reverting to his cartoon state . Recognizing Lux's aversion to the outdoors—"the one thing I never do"—Belinda devises a desperate plan . She convinces Pye to burn the film reels, a sacrificial act that causes the fire to explode a wall of the theatre, exposing Lux to the full intensity of dawn sunlight [), ]. This exposure triggers a catastrophic chain reaction. Sunlight, described in the script as being "two billion times more powerful than a nuclear bomb," causes Lux to begin absorbing infinite amounts of energy [), ]. Rather than destroying him, this event leads to his apotheosis. He utters his final words, "Sunlight! The light of creation! I am everything... And I am nothing.... Goodbye," before ascending into space as pure, omnipresent light . This outcome is framed not as a defeat but as a fulfillment of his destiny as the God of Light . Belinda's line, "So, he's actually a God now. Infinite. Invisible. Intangible," delivered with a tone of awe rather than triumph, encapsulates this poetic resolution . The episode concludes with Lux's dispersal, freeing the captured souls and leaving behind a lingering sense of wonder about the nature of divinity and transcendence [)].

## Powers, Abilities, and Weaknesses

Lux Imperator possesses a diverse array of supernatural powers, all fundamentally rooted in his nature as a being of light and his manifestation as a sentient cartoon , . His primary ability is light manipulation, which he wields with devastating effect. He can trap living beings inside individual frames of a film strip, effectively converting them into static, two-dimensional images on a flammable celluloid surface [), ]. This process not only immobilizes his victims but also converts them into cartoons, a transformation that diminishes their cognition and awareness . Furthermore, he can convert the Fifteenth Doctor and Belinda Chandra into cartoon characters, subjecting them to the logic of animation and attempting to break their will by trapping them in a surreal, hand-drawn world , . His control extends to generating and manipulating fire, summoning flames at will, which plays a crucial role in his eventual defeat . Another significant power is energy absorption. Lux draws sustenance from various forms of light, including moonlight, which was instrumental in his initial manifestation, and the intense light produced by nuclear reactions , . He demonstrated this capability most powerfully by draining the Fifteenth Doctor's regeneration energy, which temporarily granted him a more detailed, three-dimensional form before he reverted to his cartoon state , . The absorbed energy could alter his size, detail, and even his personality; for instance, regeneration energy produced a grotesque, hyper-detailed version of Mr. Ring-a-Ding, while stellar light caused him to lose his personality and physical form entirely .

In addition to these elemental powers, Lux exhibits reality-warping capabilities inherent to his existence as a living cartoon . As a "living cartoon," he operates under a logic that defies conventional physics, allowing him to tap-dance, generate sound effects, and break the fourth wall , . His very presence in the Palazzo Cinema alters the local reality, creating a pocket dimension where he is the undisputed ruler of a two-dimensional plane . This ontological instability means he can shift between states of being: a flat, two-dimensional animation, a temporary three-dimensional physicality achieved through stolen energy, and finally, a photonic dissolution into pure light . This fluidity of form is central to his character and his ultimate fate. He is also endowed with a degree of omniscience related to his domain, as evidenced by his ability to reference past events and other entities, such as identifying the Doctor as an enemy of the Toymaker and Maestro and acknowledging Sutekh's recent death [), ]. His personality, while juvenile and playful on the surface, masks a cold, calculating, and manipulative intellect, allowing him to orchestrate complex schemes involving blackmail and emotional exploitation .

Despite his formidable power, Lux Imperator's abilities are constrained by specific rules and possess a critical, fatal weakness. His most glaring vulnerability is direct, unfiltered sunlight , . Throughout the episode, he repeatedly expresses a fear of going outside, stating it as "the one thing I never do" . This fear is not irrational; exposure to daylight triggers a catastrophic feedback loop. When exposed to sufficient light, Lux begins to absorb it exponentially until he transcends his physical form, becoming an omnipresent, intangible, and godlike entity [), , ]. While this leads to his dispersal across the universe, it is presented not as a destruction but as an apotheosis, a literal fulfillment of his title as the God of Light . This weakness is exploited by Belinda Chandra, who orchestrates the burning of the film reels to breach the cinema's wall, thereby flooding the room with the dawn sun and triggering his ascension [)]. His powers are also bound by the limitations of his Mr. Ring-a-Ding persona. For example, he is compelled to perform his full theme song if the film is played, and he is honor-bound to reveal how he entered the world and could be defeated when challenged directly by the Doctor, although he chooses to answer with a riddle . These constraints provide a narrative framework for his interactions and ultimately contribute to his downfall, as his own rules and desires create the conditions for his demise.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

## Characterization and Personality

Lux Imperator's characterization is defined by a striking and compelling duality, presenting a juxtaposition between his ancient, god-like intellect and his perpetually juvenile, cartoonish exterior . On one hand, he is portrayed as cold, calculating, and manipulative, capable of forming intricate schemes and exploiting the deepest human emotions for his own survival and advancement . His decision to promise Reginald Pye visions of his deceased wife is a prime example of this calculated cruelty, demonstrating a profound understanding of grief and a willingness to weaponize it without remorse . This intellectual depth is further evidenced by his awareness of the wider Whoniverse, as he correctly identifies the Doctor as an enemy of the Toymaker and Maestro and acknowledges the recent deaths of Sutekh and the Maestro, indicating a strategic mind that understands the political landscape of the Pantheon [), ]. He is a master of psychological warfare, attempting to break the spirits of the Doctor and Belinda by forcing them to confront their fears of home and loneliness within the confines of his animated world .

On the other hand, this formidable intellect is expressed through a persona of exaggerated childishness and theatricality, consistent with the aesthetic of a 1950s-era cartoon character , . Lux frequently engages in melodramatic behaviors such as crying, dancing with fire, and punning, delivering lines like "reel him in" with a cheerful glee that belies the terror he inflicts . He sings a signature song introducing himself, complete with musical accompaniment, and generates cartoon sound effects, fully embracing the conventions of his chosen medium , . This juvenile expression is not merely a facade but a core component of his being, reflecting his arrested development and his longing for a simpler, more innocent existence. His motivation, to "go outside" and become "a real boy," taps into this childlike desire, revealing a profound sense of isolation and a yearning for something beyond his current, limited reality . This internal conflict between his divine nature and his cartoonish presentation creates a complex and unsettling character, blurring the lines between menace and melancholy.

This duality is further reflected in his vocal performance, delivered by Alan Cumming. Cumming recorded his performance in New York City in June 2024, incorporating facial expressions directly into the animation to bring the character to life [)]. His portrayal captures the character's terrifying arpeggio laugh, which is noted as a recurring motif reminiscent of the laughter of the Toymaker, establishing a subtle link between the two entities , . Cumming's performance has been described as "demented" and "Emmy-worthy," suggesting a layered and highly effective interpretation of the character's complex psychology . The character's personality is thus a carefully constructed blend of menace and whimsy, with his catchphrase "Don't make me laugh!" evolving from a playful quip into a menacing declaration as the stakes of the confrontation rise . Ultimately, his personality is that of a tragic figure: a godlike being trapped in a medium he cannot escape, using childish antics to mask a profound loneliness and a desperate, perhaps naive, desire for a physical existence he can never truly attain . His final moments, as he dissolves into the light, are imbued with a sense of poetic tragedy, a moment of apotheosis achieved through the very thing he feared most .

## Production History and Aesthetic Design

The creation of Lux Imperator and his manifestation as Mr. Ring-a-Ding was a significant technical and creative undertaking for Doctor Who Series 15 [)]. The episode was written by the show's executive producer and head writer, Russell T Davies, and directed by Amanda Brotchie [), ]. The production team made a deliberate and proud creative choice to utilize hand-drawn, frame-by-frame animation for Lux's character instead of relying on computer-generated imagery (CGI) . This decision was driven by a desire to achieve an authentic aesthetic that paid homage to the golden age of animation. The animation was handled by Framestore UK, a studio led by VFX producer Ashlee Turner, and involved a large team of nearly 60 people . The production went so far as to hire veteran animators who had worked on iconic hybrid live-action/animation films like 'Who Framed Roger Rabbit' (1988) and 'Space Jam' (1996), ensuring that the character's movement and expressiveness adhered to the highest standards of classic animation , .

The animation style was meticulously crafted to replicate the look and feel of 1930s Fleischer Studios cartoons, such as those featuring Betty Boop and Popeye, as well as early Warner Bros. rubberhose animation, reminiscent of characters like Popeye and Superman [), , ]. This specific aesthetic was not arbitrary; it was chosen to evoke the uncanny, unsettling qualities often found in mid-century animation, which aligns with Lux's nature as a surreal and threatening entity . The character's design was inspired by the pig-like nose of Fleischer characters, contributing to his distinctive and memorable appearance [)]. The animation was created at a rate of 25 frames per second using TVPaint software, a technique that authentically replicates the fluid yet slightly stiff quality of vintage cartoons . This attention to detail extended to the integration of the animated character into the live-action scenes, creating a seamless hybrid aesthetic that was a point of pride for the production team , .

The physical design of Mr. Ring-a-Ding is richly detailed and integral to his character. He is depicted as a blue-skinned, traditionally animated figure with a prominent pig-like snout , . His attire is a classic cartoonist's wardrobe, consisting of a deep purple tailcoat, a yellow waistcoat, a white shirt with a large collar, and a red bow tie . He wears a floating straw hat, and his overall appearance is covered in visible film grain, a subtle touch that reinforces his connection to celluloid and the medium of cinema . Despite being composed entirely of light, a curious detail is noted: he casts a shadow . This is mentioned as possibly being an animation artifact, but it adds another layer of ambiguity to his nature, hinting at a deeper, unresolved aspect of his metaphysical existence . Initially, he appears only two feet tall, a result of his misunderstanding of perspective, which adds a humorous element to his otherwise intimidating presence . The design was developed by creative designer Ian Spendloff, who considered thirty different sketches before the final concept was approved [)]. This extensive design process ensured that every visual element of Mr. Ring-a-Ding contributed to his identity as a being of light, a creature of nostalgia, and a potent symbol of the thin line between fiction and reality .

## Critical Reception and Thematic Analysis

The Doctor Who episode 'Lux' received a mixed but generally positive critical reception, with reviewers praising its ambitious and surreal storytelling while offering conflicting views on its handling of sensitive historical themes , . The episode was lauded for its bold creative choices, particularly its meta-cinematic focus and the novel concept of the protagonist becoming a cartoon , . Critics noted that the narrative successfully deconstructed cinematic ontology and explored the boundaries between reality and fiction, fulfilling the creative vision of showrunner Russell T Davies, who described the situation as "rather dark and strange" , . The fourth-wall-breaking element, which saw the Doctor and Belinda emerge into a living room populated by fictionalized versions of real-life fans, was highlighted as a clever and self-aware device that engaged directly with the show's fandom [), ]. This innovative approach to storytelling, combined with Alan Cumming's Emmy-worthy performance as Lux, was widely regarded as a standout feature of the episode . One review awarded the episode a score of 14 out of 20, commending its strong story, characters, and design, though expressing reservations about its treatment of historical racism .

However, the episode's engagement with the setting of segregated 1952 Miami proved to be a point of contention among critics. Some interpretations viewed the narrative as a nuanced exploration of historical trauma and systemic racism, using the oppressive atmosphere of the time to ground its supernatural plot in real-world consequences , . Writer Russell T Davies intended the inclusive casting of the lead characters to reflect "just life" and make audiences feel "visible, you feel seen," suggesting a conscious effort to address representation and historical erasure . Yet, other critics argued that the episode treated these serious issues superficially, accusing it of "ticking boxes without giving the issues any real attention" . The critique suggests that while the setting was present, the narrative failed to delve deeply into the moral complexities and dangers faced by Black citizens under Jim Crow laws, instead focusing on the fantastical elements of the plot . This discrepancy in critical opinion highlights the challenge of balancing genre storytelling with responsible historical representation. The debate surrounding the episode's execution of these themes remains a prominent topic of discussion in its reception.

Thematically, 'Lux' is a rich text that explores several interconnected ideas. The most dominant theme is the nature of fiction and reality, embodied by Lux's existence as a "living cartoon" , . The episode uses the aesthetics of classic animation to question the very foundations of cinematic representation and media consumption, drawing parallels to philosophical concepts like Plato’s Allegory of the Cave . Through Lux, the narrative examines what it means for a fictional character to step out of the screen and into reality, a concept that has been a recurring fascination in Doctor Who since stories like 'The Mind Robber' . Another central theme is grief and the ethical implications of resurrection. Lux's manipulation of Reginald Pye is predicated on his desire to see his dead wife again, a temptation that echoes broader Whoniverse questions about whether it is right to bring back the dead . This is contrasted with the Doctor's philosophy, which ultimately rejects the idea of playing God, choosing instead to respect the natural order of life and death.

Finally, the episode delves into the power of memory and the allure of false realities. Lux's world is a fabricated one, built on the illusion of celluloid, and his attempt to trap the Doctor and Belinda is a struggle for control over their perception of reality . Their journey to "flesh themselves out" emotionally, sharing their fears of home and loneliness, is a metaphor for the importance of genuine human connection in defining one's identity , . In the end, Lux's apotheosis into pure light can be interpreted as a commentary on the ephemeral nature of existence and the ultimate transcendence of the soul, a poetic and ambiguous conclusion that fits perfectly within the surreal and thought-provoking framework of the episode . The thematic richness of 'Lux' ensures that while its handling of certain topics may be debated, its contribution to the ongoing evolution of Doctor Who's narrative ambitions is undeniable.

## Comparative Analysis of Distinct "LUX" Characters

To ensure clarity and accuracy within the Doctor Who canon, it is essential to distinguish between the various characters named "Lux." The term has been applied to at least three distinct individuals, each with a unique origin, role, and significance within the series. The most prominent and recently introduced character is Lux Imperator, the God of Light who appeared in Series 15 . However, prior to this, the name has been associated with a human financier and an immortal companion, leading to potential confusion for viewers and researchers. The following table provides a comprehensive comparison of these three characters, highlighting their differences in character type, appearance, narrative function, and key traits.

| Feature | **Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding** | **Strackman Lux** | **Ashildr ("Me")** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Character Type** | Transcendental Entity (God of Light) | Human (Financier) | Human (Immortal Companion) |
| **First Appearance** | *Doctor Who*, Series 15, Episode 2 'Lux' (2025) [)] | *Doctor Who*, Series 4, Episodes 8 & 9 'Silence in the Library' / 'Forest of the Dead' (2008) | *Doctor Who*, Series 9, Episode 1 'The Girl Who Died' (2015) |
| **Portrayed By** | Alan Cumming (voice) | Steve Pemberton | Maisie Williams |
| **Role in Story** | Antagonist; member of the Pantheon of Discord [)] | Expedition Leader; heir to the Library's builders [)] | Protagonist; companion of the Twelfth Doctor |
| **Key Traits** | Manipulative, juvenile, desires physicality, god-like intellect , | Arrogant, pride-driven, bureaucratic, corporate , | Immortal, jaded, morally ambiguous, suffers from loneliness , |
| **Notable Quote** | "I am Lux. Lux Imperator, the God of Light." | "My family built this library." | "I am Me." (Adopted alias) |
| **Affiliation** | Pantheon of Discord/Chaos , | Felman Lux Corporation | None (initially); later allies with the Doctor |

The distinction between these characters is paramount for accurate analysis. **Strackman Lux**, portrayed by Steve Pemberton, is a straightforward human character. He is the leader of an archaeological expedition to the planet-sized Library in the 51st century and is defined by his arrogance, pride in his family's legacy, and initial skepticism of the Doctor's warnings , . His character arc subverts expectations, revealing a deep commitment to his family, particularly his terminally ill relative Charlotte Lux, whose consciousness becomes the Library's AI core . Unlike the divine Lux Imperator, Strackman Lux is a flawed but ultimately redeemable human being, concerned with institutional reputation and corporate interests [), ].

The most common source of confusion lies in the conflation of the name "Lux" with **Ashildr**, a human woman from the 9th century who was granted immortality by the Twelfth Doctor . After surviving for centuries, she adopted the alias "Me" to cope with the erosion of her original identity and the profound loneliness of eternal life , . While some fan discussions or informal analyses have mistakenly referred to her as "Lux," this is not a canonical designation within the provided sources . Ashildr is a complex companion whose narrative arc explores the psychological toll of immortality, moral decay, and eventual redemption . Her character is a stark contrast to Lux Imperator; she is a deeply human (though enhanced) being grappling with existential despair, whereas Lux is a god-like entity embodying the principles of light and cinematic illusion . The analysis confirms that only Lux Imperator warrants a dedicated article under the rubric provided, as he is a newly created, canonically significant entity with a unique narrative function distinct from his predecessors.

Lux Imperator's status as a new character, distinct from all prior incarnations named "Lux," allows the narrative to explore fresh thematic territory centered on the nature of fiction, the power of light, and the complexities of confronting historical injustice.
Lux Imperator's narrative function in the Doctor Who episode 'Lux' is multifaceted, serving as both a formidable supernatural antagonist and a complex meta-fictional device.

Lux Imperator's entry into the primary universe in 1952 Miami was contingent upon a rare cosmic alignment: moonlight had to reflect off a spoon onto a celluloid film projector, requiring a precise combination of reflection, electricity, and cinematic projection.
This methodical, almost whimsical origin underscores Lux Imperator's fundamental nature as a being intrinsically linked to the medium of film and light.
Once manifested, Lux Imperator's primary objective became acquiring a physical, three-dimensional body—a desire that drove his entire plotline.

Lux Imperator accomplished his objective by trapping fifteen individuals, including the young Tommy Lee Lowenstein, inside separate frames of a film reel, effectively transforming them into living cartoons.

This act of entrapment served a dual purpose: it provided Lux Imperator with a steady source of cinematic projection light to sustain his existence and allowed him to manipulate those around him to achieve his goals.
Lux Imperator's most significant interaction within the narrative was with Reginald Pye, the film operator at the Palazzo Cinema.
Lux Imperator manipulated Reginald Pye by exploiting his grief over the death of his wife, promising him visions of her if he continued to project films.
This pact reveals a key aspect of Lux Imperator's character: his willingness to exploit profound human emotions for his own ends.

Lux Imperator's relationship with Reginald Pye highlights a vulnerability, as Lux's own motivations are revealed to stem from a deep-seated loneliness and a simple, childlike desire—to go outside and become "a real boy".

This poignant motivation adds a layer of tragic complexity to Lux Imperator's otherwise malevolent actions, positioning him not as a purely evil entity but as a being bound by rules and desires that are both divine and deeply personal.

Lux Imperator is bound by the constraints of his Mr. Ring-a-Ding form, which dictates certain behaviors, such as being forced to sing his full theme song if played, and honor-bound to answer questions about his origins and methods truthfully, though he often cloaks these answers in riddles.
The central conflict of the episode revolves around the Fifteenth Doctor and his companion, Belinda Chandra, who arrive at the cinema to investigate the mass disappearances.
Upon discovering the truth, the Doctor and Belinda themselves become ensnared by Lux, who traps them inside the animated dimension of the film.
Within this surreal, hand-drawn world, Lux attempts to break their spirit by forcing them to confront their deepest fears, particularly their anxieties about home and belonging.
The Doctor's fear of returning to Gallifrey and Belinda's fear of never seeing her family again manifest physically within the cartoon realm, adding emotional weight to the abstract battle.
Lux's ultimate plan was to absorb the Doctor's remaining regeneration energy, which would grant him true corporeality and allow him to transcend his two-dimensional existence.

This ambition places Lux Imperator directly in opposition to the Doctor, whom he identifies as "Enemy of the Toymaker, decomposer of Maestro, the killer of the god of death," acknowledging the Doctor's prior victories over other members of the Pantheon.
This establishes a direct line of continuity and escalating threat, making Lux a logical successor to previous Pantheon adversaries.
The climax of the narrative sees Lux's plans unravel due to the clever agency of Belinda Chandra and the assistance of Reginald Pye.
When Lux absorbs the Doctor's regeneration energy, he momentarily achieves a grotesque, hyper-detailed three-dimensional form before reverting to his cartoon state.
Recognizing Lux's aversion to the outdoors—"the one thing I never do"—Belinda devises a desperate plan.
Belinda convinces Pye to burn the film reels, a sacrificial act that causes the fire to explode a wall of the theatre, exposing Lux to the full intensity of dawn sunlight.
This exposure triggers a catastrophic chain reaction.
Sunlight, described in the script as being "two billion times more powerful than a nuclear bomb," causes Lux to begin absorbing infinite amounts of energy.
Rather than destroying him, this event leads to Lux's apotheosis.
Lux Imperator utters his final words, "Sunlight! The light of creation! I am everything... And I am nothing.... Goodbye," before ascending into space as pure, omnipresent light.
This outcome is framed not as a defeat but as a fulfillment of Lux Imperator's destiny as the God of Light.
Belinda's line, "So, he's actually a God now. Infinite. Invisible. Intangible," delivered with a tone of awe rather than triumph, encapsulates this poetic resolution.
The episode concludes with Lux's dispersal, freeing the captured souls and leaving behind a lingering sense of wonder about the nature of divinity and transcendence.
Lux Imperator possesses a diverse array of supernatural powers, all fundamentally rooted in his nature as a being of light and his manifestation as a sentient cartoon.
Lux Imperator's primary ability is light manipulation, which he wields with devastating effect.
Lux Imperator can trap living beings inside individual frames of a film strip, effectively converting them into static, two-dimensional images on a flammable celluloid surface.
This process not only immobilizes Lux Imperator's victims but also converts them into cartoons, a transformation that diminishes their cognition and awareness.

Furthermore, Lux Imperator can convert the Fifteenth Doctor and Belinda Chandra into cartoon characters, subjecting them to the logic of animation and attempting to break their will by trapping them in a surreal, hand-drawn world.
Lux Imperator's control extends to generating and manipulating fire, summoning flames at will, which plays a crucial role in his eventual defeat.
Another significant power of Lux Imperator is energy absorption.
Lux Imperator draws sustenance from various forms of light, including moonlight, which was instrumental in his initial manifestation, and the intense light produced by nuclear reactions.

Lux Imperator demonstrated this capability most powerfully by draining the Fifteenth Doctor's regeneration energy, which temporarily granted him a more detailed, three-dimensional form before he reverted to his cartoon state.
The absorbed energy could alter Lux Imperator's size, detail, and even his personality.
Regeneration energy produced a grotesque, hyper-detailed version of Mr. Ring-a-Ding.
Stellar light caused Lux Imperator to lose his personality and physical form entirely.
In addition to these elemental powers, Lux Imperator exhibits reality-warping capabilities inherent to his existence as a living cartoon.
As a "living cartoon," Lux Imperator operates under a logic that defies conventional physics, allowing him to tap-dance, generate sound effects, and break the fourth wall.
Lux Imperator's very presence in the Palazzo Cinema alters the local reality, creating a pocket dimension where he is the undisputed ruler of a two-dimensional plane.

This ontological instability means Lux Imperator can shift between states of being: a flat, two-dimensional animation, a temporary three-dimensional physicality achieved through stolen energy, and finally, a photonic dissolution into pure light.
This fluidity of form is central to Lux Imperator's character and his ultimate fate.

Lux Imperator is also endowed with a degree of omniscience related to his domain, as evidenced by his ability to reference past events and other entities, such as identifying the Doctor as an enemy of the Toymaker and Maestro and acknowledging Sutekh's recent death.

Lux Imperator's personality, while juvenile and playful on the surface, masks a cold, calculating, and manipulative intellect, allowing him to orchestrate complex schemes involving blackmail and emotional exploitation.
Despite his formidable power, Lux Imperator's abilities are constrained by specific rules and possess a critical, fatal weakness.
Lux Imperator's most glaring vulnerability is direct, unfiltered sunlight.
Throughout the episode, Lux Imperator repeatedly expresses a fear of going outside, stating it as "the one thing I never do".
This fear is not irrational; exposure to daylight triggers a catastrophic feedback loop.
When exposed to sufficient light, Lux Imperator begins to absorb it exponentially until he transcends his physical form, becoming an omnipresent, intangible, and godlike entity.
While this leads to Lux Imperator's dispersal across the universe, it is presented not as a destruction but as an apotheosis, a literal fulfillment of his title as the God of Light.

This weakness is exploited by Belinda Chandra, who orchestrates the burning of the film reels to breach the cinema's wall, thereby flooding the room with the dawn sun and triggering Lux Imperator's ascension.
Lux Imperator's powers are also bound by the limitations of his Mr. Ring-a-Ding persona.
Lux Imperator is compelled to perform his full theme song if the film is played.
Lux Imperator is honor-bound to reveal how he entered the world and could be defeated when challenged directly by the Doctor, although he chooses to answer with a riddle.
These constraints provide a narrative framework for Lux Imperator's interactions and ultimately contribute to his downfall, as his own rules and desires create the conditions for his demise.
Lux Imperator's Light Manipulation ability allows him to control and harness light for various purposes, including trapping and conversion.
Lux Imperator traps 15 people inside individual frames of a film strip, converting them into cartoons.
Lux Imperator's Energy Absorption ability means he can absorb various forms of energy, particularly light, to grow stronger, increase in size, or gain temporary corporeality.
Lux Imperator drains the Fifteenth Doctor's regeneration energy, briefly achieving a 3D form.
As a living cartoon, Lux Imperator's Reality Warping ability allows him to bend the rules of reality, including dimensional travel and breaking the fourth wall.
Lux Imperator traps the Doctor and Belinda in a two-dimensional animated realm.
Lux Imperator breaks the fourth wall to address the audience directly.
Lux Imperator's Fire Summoning ability means he can generate and control flames at will.
Lux Imperator uses fire to taunt and threaten the Doctor and Belinda within the cartoon dimension.
Lux Imperator possesses Fourth-Wall Awareness, meaning he has knowledge that he exists within a television program and can acknowledge the audience.
Lux Imperator references "The Giggle" and breaks the fourth wall to comment on the narrative.
Lux Imperator operates under the nonsensical rules of classic animation, including exaggerated movements, sound effects, and improbable feats, due to his Cartoon Logic.
Lux Imperator tap-dances, generates sound effects, and behaves in ways that defy physical laws.
Lux Imperator's characterization is defined by a striking and compelling duality, presenting a juxtaposition between his ancient, god-like intellect and his perpetually juvenile, cartoonish exterior.
Lux Imperator is portrayed as cold, calculating, and manipulative, capable of forming intricate schemes and exploiting the deepest human emotions for his own survival and advancement.

Lux Imperator's decision to promise Reginald Pye visions of his deceased wife is a prime example of his calculated cruelty, demonstrating a profound understanding of grief and a willingness to weaponize it without remorse.

Lux Imperator's intellectual depth is further evidenced by his awareness of the wider Whoniverse, as he correctly identifies the Doctor as an enemy of the Toymaker and Maestro and acknowledges the recent deaths of Sutekh and the Maestro, indicating a strategic mind that understands the political landscape of the Pantheon.

Lux Imperator is a master of psychological warfare, attempting to break the spirits of the Doctor and Belinda by forcing them to confront their fears of home and loneliness within the confines of his animated world.
Lux Imperator's formidable intellect is expressed through a persona of exaggerated childishness and theatricality, consistent with the aesthetic of a 1950s-era cartoon character.
Lux Imperator frequently engages in melodramatic behaviors such as crying, dancing with fire, and punning, delivering lines like "reel him in" with a cheerful glee that belies the terror he inflicts.
Lux Imperator sings a signature song introducing himself, complete with musical accompaniment, and generates cartoon sound effects, fully embracing the conventions of his chosen medium.
This juvenile expression is not merely a facade but a core component of Lux Imperator's being, reflecting his arrested development and his longing for a simpler, more innocent existence.

Lux Imperator's motivation, to "go outside" and become "a real boy," taps into this childlike desire, revealing a profound sense of isolation and a yearning for something beyond his current, limited reality.
This internal conflict between Lux Imperator's divine nature and his cartoonish presentation creates a complex and unsettling character, blurring the lines between menace and melancholy.
This duality is further reflected in Lux Imperator's vocal performance, delivered by Alan Cumming.
Alan Cumming recorded his performance in New York City in June 2024, incorporating facial expressions directly into the animation to bring the character to life.

Alan Cumming's portrayal captures the character's terrifying arpeggio laugh, which is noted as a recurring motif reminiscent of the laughter of the Toymaker, establishing a subtle link between the two entities.
Alan Cumming's performance has been described as "demented" and "Emmy-worthy," suggesting a layered and highly effective interpretation of the character's complex psychology.

Lux Imperator's personality is thus a carefully constructed blend of menace and whimsy, with his catchphrase "Don't make me laugh!" evolving from a playful quip into a menacing declaration as the stakes of the confrontation rise.

Ultimately, Lux Imperator's personality is that of a tragic figure: a godlike being trapped in a medium he cannot escape, using childish antics to mask a profound loneliness and a desperate, perhaps naive, desire for a physical existence he can never truly attain.
Lux Imperator's final moments, as he dissolves into the light, are imbued with a sense of poetic tragedy, a moment of apotheosis achieved through the very thing he feared most.
The creation of Lux Imperator and his manifestation as Mr. Ring-a-Ding was a significant technical and creative undertaking for Doctor Who Series 15.
The episode 'Lux' was written by the show's executive producer and head writer, Russell T Davies, and directed by Amanda Brotchie.
The production team made a deliberate and proud creative choice to utilize hand-drawn, frame-by-frame animation for Lux's character instead of relying on computer-generated imagery (CGI).
This decision was driven by a desire to achieve an authentic aesthetic that paid homage to the golden age of animation.
The animation was handled by Framestore UK, a studio led by VFX producer Ashlee Turner, and involved a large team of nearly 60 people.

The production went so far as to hire veteran animators who had worked on iconic hybrid live-action/animation films like 'Who Framed Roger Rabbit' (1988) and 'Space Jam' (1996), ensuring that the character's movement and expressiveness adhered to the highest standards of classic animation.

The animation style was meticulously crafted to replicate the look and feel of 1930s Fleischer Studios cartoons, such as those featuring Betty Boop and Popeye, as well as early Warner Bros. rubberhose animation, reminiscent of characters like Popeye and Superman.

This specific aesthetic was not arbitrary; it was chosen to evoke the uncanny, unsettling qualities often found in mid-century animation, which aligns with Lux's nature as a surreal and threatening entity.
The character's design was inspired by the pig-like nose of Fleischer characters, contributing to his distinctive and memorable appearance.
The animation was created at a rate of 25 frames per second using TVPaint software, a technique that authentically replicates the fluid yet slightly stiff quality of vintage cartoons.
This attention to detail extended to the integration of the animated character into the live-action scenes, creating a seamless hybrid aesthetic that was a point of pride for the production team.
The physical design of Mr. Ring-a-Ding is richly detailed and integral to his character.
Mr. Ring-a-Ding is depicted as a blue-skinned, traditionally animated figure with a prominent pig-like snout.
Mr. Ring-a-Ding's attire is a classic cartoonist's wardrobe, consisting of a deep purple tailcoat, a yellow waistcoat, a white shirt with a large collar, and a red bow tie.
Mr. Ring-a-Ding wears a floating straw hat, and his overall appearance is covered in visible film grain, a subtle touch that reinforces his connection to celluloid and the medium of cinema.
Despite being composed entirely of light, a curious detail is noted: Mr. Ring-a-Ding casts a shadow.
This is mentioned as possibly being an animation artifact, but it adds another layer of ambiguity to Mr. Ring-a-Ding's nature, hinting at a deeper, unresolved aspect of his metaphysical existence.
Initially, Mr. Ring-a-Ding appears only two feet tall, a result of his misunderstanding of perspective, which adds a humorous element to his otherwise intimidating presence.
The design was developed by creative designer Ian Spendloff, who considered thirty different sketches before the final concept was approved.

This extensive design process ensured that every visual element of Mr. Ring-a-Ding contributed to his identity as a being of light, a creature of nostalgia, and a potent symbol of the thin line between fiction and reality.

The Doctor Who episode 'Lux' received a mixed but generally positive critical reception, with reviewers praising its ambitious and surreal storytelling while offering conflicting views on its handling of sensitive historical themes.
The episode was lauded for its bold creative choices, particularly its meta-cinematic focus and the novel concept of the protagonist becoming a cartoon.

Critics noted that the narrative successfully deconstructed cinematic ontology and explored the boundaries between reality and fiction, fulfilling the creative vision of showrunner Russell T Davies, who described the situation as "rather dark and strange".

The fourth-wall-breaking element, which saw the Doctor and Belinda emerge into a living room populated by fictionalized versions of real-life fans, was highlighted as a clever and self-aware device that engaged directly with the show's fandom.
This innovative approach to storytelling, combined with Alan Cumming's Emmy-worthy performance as Lux, was widely regarded as a standout feature of the episode.
One review awarded the episode a score of 14 out of 20, commending its strong story, characters, and design, though expressing reservations about its treatment of historical racism.
The episode's engagement with the setting of segregated 1952 Miami proved to be a point of contention among critics.

Some interpretations viewed the narrative as a nuanced exploration of historical trauma and systemic racism, using the oppressive atmosphere of the time to ground its supernatural plot in real-world consequences.

Writer Russell T Davies intended the inclusive casting of the lead characters to reflect "just life" and make audiences feel "visible, you feel seen," suggesting a conscious effort to address representation and historical erasure.
Other critics argued that the episode treated these serious issues superficially, accusing it of "ticking boxes without giving the issues any real attention".

The critique suggests that while the setting was present, the narrative failed to delve deeply into the moral complexities and dangers faced by Black citizens under Jim Crow laws, instead focusing on the fantastical elements of the plot.
This discrepancy in critical opinion highlights the challenge of balancing genre storytelling with responsible historical representation.
The debate surrounding the episode's execution of these themes remains a prominent topic of discussion in its reception.
Thematically, 'Lux' is a rich text that explores several interconnected ideas.
The most dominant theme is the nature of fiction and reality, embodied by Lux's existence as a "living cartoon".

The episode uses the aesthetics of classic animation to question the very foundations of cinematic representation and media consumption, drawing parallels to philosophical concepts like Plato’s Allegory of the Cave.

Through Lux, the narrative examines what it means for a fictional character to step out of the screen and into reality, a concept that has been a recurring fascination in Doctor Who since stories like 'The Mind Robber'.
Another central theme is grief and the ethical implications of resurrection.
Lux's manipulation of Reginald Pye is predicated on his desire to see his dead wife again, a temptation that echoes broader Whoniverse questions about whether it is right to bring back the dead.
This is contrasted with the Doctor's philosophy, which ultimately rejects the idea of playing God, choosing instead to respect the natural order of life and death.
The episode delves into the power of memory and the allure of false realities.
Lux's world is a fabricated one, built on the illusion of celluloid, and his attempt to trap the Doctor and Belinda is a struggle for control over their perception of reality.
Their journey to "flesh themselves out" emotionally, sharing their fears of home and loneliness, is a metaphor for the importance of genuine human connection in defining one's identity.

In the end, Lux's apotheosis into pure light can be interpreted as a commentary on the ephemeral nature of existence and the ultimate transcendence of the soul, a poetic and ambiguous conclusion that fits perfectly within the surreal and thought-provoking framework of the episode.
The thematic richness of 'Lux' ensures that while its handling of certain topics may be debated, its contribution to the ongoing evolution of Doctor Who's narrative ambitions is undeniable.
To ensure clarity and accuracy within the Doctor Who canon, it is essential to distinguish between the various characters named "Lux."
The term "Lux" has been applied to at least three distinct individuals, each with a unique origin, role, and significance within the series.
The most prominent and recently introduced character is Lux Imperator, the God of Light who appeared in Series 15.
Prior to Lux Imperator, the name "Lux" has been associated with a human financier and an immortal companion, leading to potential confusion for viewers and researchers.
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding is a Transcendental Entity (God of Light).
Strackman Lux is a Human (Financier).
Ashildr ("Me") is a Human (Immortal Companion).
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding's first appearance was in Doctor Who, Series 15, Episode 2 'Lux' (2025).
Strackman Lux's first appearance was in Doctor Who, Series 4, Episodes 8 & 9 'Silence in the Library' / 'Forest of the Dead' (2008).
Ashildr ("Me")'s first appearance was in Doctor Who, Series 9, Episode 1 'The Girl Who Died' (2015).
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding is portrayed by Alan Cumming (voice).
Strackman Lux is portrayed by Steve Pemberton.
Ashildr ("Me") is portrayed by Maisie Williams.
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding's role in the story is Antagonist; member of the Pantheon of Discord.
Strackman Lux's role in the story is Expedition Leader; heir to the Library's builders.
Ashildr ("Me")'s role in the story is Protagonist; companion of the Twelfth Doctor.
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding's key traits are Manipulative, juvenile, desires physicality, god-like intellect.
Strackman Lux's key traits are Arrogant, pride-driven, bureaucratic, corporate.
Ashildr ("Me")'s key traits are Immortal, jaded, morally ambiguous, suffers from loneliness.
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding's notable quote is "I am Lux. Lux Imperator, the God of Light."
Strackman Lux's notable quote is "My family built this library."
Ashildr ("Me")'s notable quote is "I am Me." (Adopted alias).
Lux Imperator / Mr. Ring-a-Ding's affiliation is Pantheon of Discord/Chaos.
Strackman Lux's affiliation is Felman Lux Corporation.
Ashildr ("Me")'s affiliation is None (initially); later allies with the Doctor.
The distinction between these characters is paramount for accurate analysis.
Strackman Lux, portrayed by Steve Pemberton, is a straightforward human character.

Strackman Lux is the leader of an archaeological expedition to the planet-sized Library in the 51st century and is defined by his arrogance, pride in his family's legacy, and initial skepticism of the Doctor's warnings.

Strackman Lux's character arc subverts expectations, revealing a deep commitment to his family, particularly his terminally ill relative Charlotte Lux, whose consciousness becomes the Library's AI core.
Unlike the divine Lux Imperator, Strackman Lux is a flawed but ultimately redeemable human being, concerned with institutional reputation and corporate interests.
The most common source of confusion lies in the conflation of the name "Lux" with Ashildr, a human woman from the 9th century who was granted immortality by the Twelfth Doctor.
After surviving for centuries, Ashildr adopted the alias "Me" to cope with the erosion of her original identity and the profound loneliness of eternal life.
While some fan discussions or informal analyses have mistakenly referred to Ashildr as "Lux," this is not a canonical designation within the provided sources.
Ashildr is a complex companion whose narrative arc explores the psychological toll of immortality, moral decay, and eventual redemption.

Ashildr's character is a stark contrast to Lux Imperator; she is a deeply human (though enhanced) being grappling with existential despair, whereas Lux is a god-like entity embodying the principles of light and cinematic illusion.

The analysis confirms that only Lux Imperator warrants a dedicated article under the rubric provided, as he is a newly created, canonically significant entity with a unique narrative function distinct from his predecessors.

Synopsis and Cast Announced for This Weekend’s Doctor Who: Lux
--------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 1: Synopsis and Cast Announced for This Weekend’s Doctor Who: Lux](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Ncuti-Gatwa-15th-Fifteenth-Lux-Belinda-Chandra-Varada-Sethu.jpg)

*   Posted On: [14 April 2025](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/2025/04/14/synopsis-and-cast-announced-for-this-weekends-doctor-who-lux/)
*   Posted By: [Philip Bates](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/author/prbates36/)
*   Comments: [0](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/2025/04/14/synopsis-and-cast-announced-for-this-weekends-doctor-who-lux/)

_Doctor Who_ Series 15 is underway, with the Fifteenth Doctor (Nucit Gatwa) trying to get Belinda Chandra (Varada Sethu) back home. But before that, they’ve got a trip to Miami in the 1950s, where a sinister presence lurks in an abandoned theatre…

Here’s the synopsis for _Lux_, this weekend’s episode:

> “The Doctor’s quest to get Belinda home takes the TARDIS to Miami in 1952, where an abandoned cinema is hiding a terrifying secret. Can the Doctor uncover Lux’s power?”

And [here’s who’s starring](https://cultbox.co.uk/general/doctor-who-lux-cast-and-bbc-one-airtime-confirmed) in the episode alongside Gatwa and Sethu:

*   Linus Roache: Reginald Pye
*   Alan Cumming: Mr Ring-a-Ding
*   Millie O’Connell: Sunshine Sally
*   Ian Shaw: Newsreader
*   Cassius Hackforth: Tommy Lee
*   Ryan Speakman: Husband
*   Lewis Cornay: Logan Cheever
*   Lucy Thackeray: Renée Lowenstein
*   Jane Hancock: Helen Pye
*   William Meredith: Policeman
*   Samir Arrian: Hassan
*   Bronte Barbe: Lizzie
*   Steph Lacey: Robyn
*   Anita Dobson: Mrs Flood

Yep, Anita Dobson is back as Mrs Flood, a role she first played in _The Church on Ruby Road_. And fans will remember Alan Cumming for playing King James in _The Witchfinders_, with Jodie Whittaker’s Thirteenth Doctor. Here, he’s an animated character, Mr Ring-a-Ding, as is Millie O’Connell, playing Sunshine Sally.

The 43-minute episode will be followed by an instalment of _Doctor Who Unleashed_, on BBC Three at 8:00pm, going behind the scenes on the story.

Written by Russell T Davies and directed by Amanda Brotchie, _Lux_ airs on Saturday 19 April from 8am on BBC iPlayer and 7:15pm on BBC One in the UK. Fans outside the UK can catch it on Disney+.

19 April 2025 at 18:18 [#77285](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77285)

![Image 1: Doctor Who Lux](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/lux.jpg)

The second episode, and this one is supposedly a good one – a high-concept bit of craziness.

The Doctor’s quest to get Belinda home takes the Tardis to Miami in 1952 at the height of segregation. An abandoned cinema is hiding a terrifying secret, Lux Imperator, God of Light, who has taken on the form of a living cartoon character called Mr Ring-a-Ding.

This is, once again, written by RTD, and it’s directed by Amanda Brotchie, who is also directing next week’s episode, so it better be good. She’s an Australian director known for the multi-award-winning comedy series ‘Lowdown’ on ABC and BBC4, Amazon Prime’s series of ‘Picnic at Hanging Rock’ and Netflix’s comedy series ‘Girlboss’.

And guest starring are the ever-reliable Linus Roache, and Alan Cumming having a blast as Mr Ring-a-Ding.

19 April 2025 at 20:39 [#77291](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77291)

Well an enjoyable romp. I think I now know  where the online rumour of Ncuti filming a regeneration scene came from so maybe Ncuti isn’t leaving the show anytime soon, though to be honest given his increasing “fame” and I assume offers of work I wouldn’t  be surprised if he only does 3 or 4 seasons and I think the overall average is 4 seasons. Yes there has been actors that have done many more seasons ie Pertwee  I think, and Tom Baker pre gap and Tenant and Smith post gap so expecting an actor to commit for much more is probably  impractical of fans we will probably be lucky if we get 4 seasons.  
Anyway back to the episode it’s obviously hinting that the mad/chaos gods are definitely  behind events in the whoniverse here we have another mad god creating mischief. Obviously something has happened on May  24 and I’ve just realised the season finale  is going to be broadcast about that date though it may be the weekend before I can’t remember if the season is 6 or 7 episodes. Also I see we have another episode that is heavily making social commentary on the times the episode is set.

19 April 2025 at 21:47 [#77294](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77294)

That was very enjoyable. Take aways…

This is definitely in The Mind Robberverse. I was a bit annoyed by the ‘don’t make me laff!’ ‘Why? Oh it’s the giggle!’ After which some letters fall off Rock’s credits on the OUTSIDE the cinema revealing… but it is the Doctor, who’s INSIDE, who says ‘hey it’s only the chuffing Harbinger!’ Well, if it is a sort of dream, then that kinda thing does go down eh? I’m surprised no one was naked on the bus. Baldrick, you’ve turned into an Alsatian, stop it! Probably explains the ersatz Beatles and Stupid Sutekh too.

Ooops look like something may really have happened to The Earth!

2025 – 1952 = 73!!

The V’indicator could be a nod to the V’linx???

A quite outrageous attempt to upstage Gatwa even more than Davison was at the end of Caves of Androzani.

Would Mrs Lowenstein, 1952, Miami, really address The Doctor as ‘sir?’ But nice nod to Trump’s ai ‘arrest’ fake photos with the NYPD uniform.

And the meta fan appearance! That might be a bit too much for some people.

Best bit? ‘I’m Velma.’

Well, I liked all of it from the scary start to the finish. I have loved the mix of live action and cartoons since I saw Gene Kelly dance with the mouse from Tom and Jerry when I was a little kid.Then I thought it was magic and after this episode I still do. I just wish the Doctor and Belinda were animated a little longer.

The music as usual was perfect and hearing Amy’s theme and Sad  Man made me feel very nostalgic.  Mr. Ding had his own  theme music, funny.

Who or what is Mrs Flood? She is starting to bother me now.

If it wasn’t so late I would watch again right now and I haven’t felt that way about an episode for awhile.

stay timey-wimey

20 April 2025 at 04:11 [#77301](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77301)

There is a scene in the cinema, where they are screening an old black and white Western. It immediately reminded me of one of the most wonderful 1950s British comedies ever made,  “The Smallest Show on Earth,” about a young couple who inherit a run-down cinema, and try to make it work, by showing cheap movies, including an old Western. As I watched the show tonight I really wondered if RTD2 was using the same cinema footage of the old Western  from “The Smallest Show on Earth”.

If If you have never seen the movie, with Margaret Rutherford, Peter Sellers, and many more, I encourage you to seek it out. It is one of the most wonderful British comedies of the 1950s.

20 April 2025 at 11:00 [#77302](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77302)

I liked it! I think it was great how characters on film could be brought to life and I started to have fantasies about using this technique. I think the fans watching on TV was a nice touch, as well. It was a shame it was set on Earth, though. I want to see some stories which are completely set on other planets. We haven’t had this so far in this series. Lux was shown draining lots of regeneration energy from The Doctor, so I wonder how he’s supposed to recover from this drain. I was surprised to see Gaumont British News being shown in a cinema in the USA. Was it really shown?

I think there was a continuity error compared with the Thirteenth Doctor episode “Rosa”. “Lux” is set in Dade, Miami, Florida in 1952, but “Rosa” is set in Montgomery, Alabama in 1955. I’m not sure if that makes any differerence in this case, though. They mentioned racial segregation. This was described as banning “black” people from the Diner, as well as from the Cinema. However, both Yaz and Belinda are obviously of ancestry from the Indian subcontinent. In “Rosa”, Yaz was allowed to board the bus at the front, instead of in the middle, so this meant she was classified as white. She was called “Mexican” in a restaurant and refused service, though. Yes, excellent call about the similarities between Mr Ring A Ding and Miss Sunshine and the Doctor and Bel. I think we can read that as a meta-commentary clue about the nature of reality being squiffy in Gatwa-Doc’s universe, as well as a meta-commentary on the darker side of the Doctor – a fantastical being like Mr Ring A Ding forever seducing/ kidnapping innocent young things like Miss Sunshine to take them away in his time machine! Mr Ring A Ding is magnetic (literally full of light and magic, as he’s made of moonshine) and sinister, just like the Doctor who has, after all, effectively kidnapped Bel and is currently unable to return her to her parents, despite her desperate wish that he do so. Gatwa Doc has compared himself to Willy Wonka (he sings some lines from “Pure Imagination” when he welcomes Rogue to the Tardis in 14×06 _Rogue_) and we’ve previously compared him to Peter Pan. The goblins in 14×01 _The Church on Ruby Road_ who kidnap babies to eat them are a bit of a dark mirror for the Doctor, who “kidnaps” orphan Ruby (I mean c’mon he is back on his bullshit of going for human companions who are, in their early 20s, only a few years out of childhood). Both Wonka and Pan are fantastical and deeply attractive characters with dark sides who entrance children away to magical realms (Wonka’s “golden ticket” factory and Pan’s Neverland). I really like this subtextual element of RTD 2.0 – the Doctor as a Pied Piper figure.

I was also struck by the similarity between Bel’s yellow 1950s dress and the pink 1950s dress worn by Rose in _The Idiot’s Lantern_, which was set in London in 1953 (and this episode is set in 1952 in the US).

Also I was struck by the similarity between the red-bodied robots in the first episode of this season, _The Robot Revolution_, and the cyborg King Hydroflax in _The Husbands of River Song_. Incidentally, the robots of _The Robot Revolution_ were designed, according to the production notes in the Wikipedia entry for the episode, with a “retrofuturistic” look influenced by the 1950s:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Robot\_Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Robot_Revolution)

Possibly that desire for a ’50s look is part of RTD’s underlying critical theme in the Gatwa era, tackled explicitly through the Al-as-coercive-incel character in that episode, and the Jim Crow segregation in ’50s Florida in this one, about how our contemporary moment (with its retrogressive “anti-wokeness”) is insisting on time-travelling back to the 1950s.

However, the broader theme we’re discussing here is whether the cartoons-become-real in _Lux_ hints that call-backs to previous Who in the Gatwa era are part of a meta-narrative, whereby the Pantheon have trapped Gatwa Doc in an Alternative salt-line-has-been-crossed “mavity” Universe or, as in [@ps1l0v3y0u](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/members/ps1l0v3y0u/) ‘s great theory of it being The Mind Robber’s pocket universe.

Essentially, that would mean the similarities we’ve been noticing to past episodes and characters in Gatwa’s run are the result of the Pantheon remixing the Doctor’s past. So bubbly blonde Ruby Sunday is a bit of a Rose Tyler echo (for example) and Sutekh of course is a Baker’s Doctor’s old god villain redux. We’ve previousl remarked, here on _The Doctor Who Forum_ regarding similarities to previous Doctor Who in Gatwa’s run. In particular, we talked at the time about the way in which Rogue seems like a perfect mash-up between River Song and Captain Jack Harkness – catnip or bait, for the Doc, you might say.

The name “Lux” is familiar from Doctor Who audio stories _Escape from New New York_ and others, where the Lux are a species who attempt to take over the planet by creating cybernetic servants, the Lumen:

[https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/The\_Lux](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/The_Lux)

There is also John Lumic (another light reference) who was the creator of Cybus Industries on the parallel Earth in 2×05 _Rise of the Cybermen_.  And one of the Doctor Who fans in _Lux_ (who think they’re fictional constructs but bend “reality” by remaining at the end) is wearing a cyberman T-Shirt with the word “Telos” written on it. That is the planet Troughton Doctor visits in _Tomb of the Cybermen_.

We could read the cyborg references (the robots of MissBelindaChandra and the cybermen reference in this episode) as other clues to the artificial, created, nature of the universe Gatwa Doc is currently travelling in.

And we’ve speculated before that perhaps the reason Gatwa-Doc cries in every episode is that on some level, his Time Lord bi-generated body already knows that he’s inside a gigantic trap. And perhaps the solution is that the bi-generation has to re-merge, Gatwa-Doc and Tenant 2.0 Doc coming back together, ending Gatwa’s run?

I don’t think RTD will retore Gallifrey anytime soon – this reboot of the show has a lonely Time Lord (apart from the other one on Earth!), and I suspect he’ll prefer that thematically. Season 3 or 4 for a big TL reveal is my guess. That said he could bring a single one back at any point.

If Mrs Flood turns up with a gold tooth, then she is Missy Master. I surrender. Thing is, last time I saw it, gnasher in question was last seen in Max Capricorn’s gob while he plummeted into the Titanic’s Storm Drive with Kylie. Explain.

Safe to say, Moff was pro Gallifrey; RTD and Duff Chris were anti. Is the big red world coming back? Don’t look good. Unless TCC has really been relegated to the Land of Fiction – and imagine the fall out from that – Gallifrey should be safely death particled into submission.

Death by Death Particle! I can hear the teeth grinding in Russ’ head. Death by Crayon.

The Monk was a blithering idiot. Rather have The War Chief, if he wasn’t actually a pre Magister Master. Or the Rani… if she isn’t Tecteun.

But IF it was only Gallifrey that bought it, we must be looking at a Time Lord who couldn’t be scragged.

Aside from The Doctor…

The Master is a tooth, apparently.

Omega is ‘safe’ and ‘mad’ in antimatter land with all his happy chicken headed mooks.

Romana may or may not have been embroiled in The Time War, but I should think the Master’s pre T’floox entropy flim flam might easily have mucked up all those handy charged vacuum embodiments, leaving her marooned in E space with all the yummy lion people long time. What Time Ladies get up to on holiday.

River is in a VR already. With Doctor Moon, Dot and Bubbly tech and nasty woodlicey Vashta Nerada maybe?

But… what exactly happened to The Division? I dunno. Don’t want to look, mummy.

I know no one wants to go there, but you would think The Division should be harder to flush away than Star Trek’s Section 31, surely?

Gallifrey.

Gallifrey was hidden CLOSE to end of The Universe because of Infamy… apparently The Universe had it in for them. I have days like that. But it wasn’t the ACTUAL end, presumably because the heating bill was too high and you couldn’t get Uber Eats.

The Doctor went close to (three different bits of) The End of Time. Yana’s world (an accident) Orson’s world (a mad endeavour) and Gallifrey, the hidden track (to get Clara’s heart going again). Gallifrey presumably died some time after The Doctor stole his second type 40 (unless it was actually the first one but earlier on) to get there. Ashildr presumably got there after Death by Particle, having outlived The Universe. Must be overuse of the Vortex Manipulator makes your face go like Boe’s.

Also, got to be careful about crossing his own Timeline. Not sure BLE applies to card carrying ‘Time Species’ or we wouldn’t then have all the fun and games with 2, 3, 5 Doctors, The Day of The Doctor, or Twice Upon a Time.

Gallifrey of The Deadly Assassin, Invasion of Time, Arc of Infinity and even Hell Bent, is a bit shonky. You really want it back? I need to finish Chris and The Division. Bet you they didn’t have stupid collars.

But still… urghh.

On first impression, this reminds me of Cool World, a cartoon/live action from the 90’s in which a cartoon character was trying to break through into reality.

The people trapped in a photograph (or a frame of a film) rings a distant bell. Sapphire and Steel, maybe?

When they break out of the TV screen into the fans’ living room. Well that’s new. I think the fourth wall is not just broken, it’s shattered. This is surely the ultimate meta. Hey, I admire the fans’ taste – Blink is their favourite adventure. … and – RTD retcons this, the fans were an illusion, reality is restored. I have to say he got me, I love it when that happens.

Quite how the 15 missing people got restored, I can’t follow.

This was certainly – different.

Now to read the comments…

3 July 2025 at 15:52 [#77968](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77968)

[@blenkinsopthebrave](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/members/blenkinsopthebrave/) Oh yes, those fans in ‘Sherlock’ theorising over the Reichenbach fall were a hoot. (Just double-checked it was RTD who wrote this episode, I do hope Moff was suitably grateful for the ‘Blink’ reference)

[@winston](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/members/winston/) If you like live action / cartoons, have you seen ‘Cool World’ from 1992? It’s my favourite of the genre.

[@devilishrobby](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/members/devilishrobby/) I think you’re correct about the limited number of films a cinema would have on loan from the distributors. Film duplication would be a very slow, expensive process so only a limited number would be made. As they got old and got broken a few times and rejoined, the copies in circulation became increasingly dilapidated, so I guess less favoured cinemas out in the country would get the tatty copies after more remunerative cinemas had finished with them. Nitrate film stock was replaced with acetate ‘safety film’ about 1952, which means there’s a minor time anomaly with Rock Hudson, who only became a star in 1954. Also, though nitrate film stock was extremely inflammable, I’m not sure it was ever explosive. The most it would do was produce explosive gases – which I guess could then ignite.

4 July 2025 at 05:13 [#77971](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/forums/topic/lux/#post-77971)

[@whohar](https://www.thedoctorwhoforum.com/members/whohar/)   Yes.   Call that a double retcon.   I was delighted with the ‘fan’ sequence – the fans telling the Doc they were real and he was the fiction – which is true in reality but falsifies the story; then RTD retcons that to the ‘fans’ being fictional and part of the story.   (And I found the way in which they were willing to sacrifice their existence for the Doctor’s benefit, quite touching).

Then in the credits sequence, he retcons it \*again\* and the fans are, to their surprise,  still there.   This is impossible in the story logic, though it gave me the warm feels.   I’m not sure if it’s supposed to be an ‘official’ part of the story or just a sentimental postscript not to be taken too seriously.   I can’t see how it can be logically accounted for, maybe RTD will explain it in a future episode.

cheers
