The Pantheon of Gods has returned in [Doctor Who's](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-season-15-release-date/) newest episode in an unexpected way - with a menacing cartoon character.

Mr Ring-a-Ding, the animated character voiced by Alan Cumming, reveals himself to be Lux Imperator, the god of light and one of the Pantheon, and attempts to steal light from the Doctor's (Ncuti Gatwa) remaining bigeneration energy.

Thankfully, the Doctor and [Belinda (Varada Sethu)](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-belinda-mundy-flynn-exclusive-newsupdate/) manage to defeat Lux with the help of Reginald Pye (Linus Roache) - but we have a feeling that's not the last we'll see of the Pantheon.

Here's everything you need to know about them!

**What is the Pantheon in Doctor Who?**
---------------------------------------

The Pantheon is a group of gods/transcendental beings who have made it their mission to alter reality and cause chaos.

It consists of:

*   [**Lux**](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-lux-alan-cumming-explained/)
*   [**The Celestial Toymaker**](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-toymaker-neil-patrick-harris-explained/)
*   [**Maestro**](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-jinkx-monsoon-maestro-explained/)
*   [**Sutekh**](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/sutekh-doctor-who-one-who-waits/)
*   [**The Mara**](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-mara-meddling-monk-return/)
*   [**The Trickster**](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/doctor-who-pantheon-gods-trickster-explained/)
*   **Reprobate**
*   **Malice, Mischief and Misery**
*   **Gods of Skin and Shame and Secrets**
*   **Incensor**
*   **Dread and Doubt**

Read on for more information about the gods we've seen so far.

**Lux**
-------

![Image 4: Lux/Mr Ring-a-Ding in Doctor Who episode Lux smiling](https://images.immediate.co.uk/production/volatile/sites/3/2025/04/516704-1248701-e1744904880441.jpg?quality=90&fit=700,466)

Lux/Mr Ring-a-Ding in Doctor Who episode Lux. BBC Studios/Bad Wolf

Lux Imperator (voiced by Alan Cumming) is the god of light, and disguised himself as cartoon character Mr Ring-a-Ding.

The Doctor and Belinda defeated him by drowning him in light and making him invisible and intangible.

**The Celestial Toymaker**
--------------------------

![Image 5: Neil Patrick Harris as the Toymaker in Doctor Who in a toy shop](https://images.immediate.co.uk/production/volatile/sites/3/2023/09/p0ggbkv1-a7e6ad1.jpg?quality=90&fit=700,467)

Neil Patrick Harris as the Toymaker in Doctor Who. BBC

The Toymaker (played by Michael Gough in the show's classic era and then by Neil Patrick Harris) is a celestial being known for his games and traps, and using people as his playthings.

The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Doctors (David Tennant and Gatwa) defeated the Toymaker in The Giggle by challenging the Toymaker to - and winning - a simple game of catch.

**Maestro**
-----------

![Image 6: Jinkx Monsoon as Maestro in Doctor Who hanging over a piano with an evil and mischievous look.](https://images.immediate.co.uk/production/volatile/sites/3/2024/04/475614-bd193a8.jpg?quality=90&fit=700,467)

Jinkx Monsoon as Maestro in Doctor Who. BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon

Played by Jinkx Monsoon, Maestro is the god of music and has control over all melodies in the universe.

The Doctor and Ruby Sunday (Millie Gibson) defeated Maestro in The Devil's Chord with the help of the Beatles, who completed the one chord that can trap the god inside their piano.

**Sutekh**
----------

![Image 7: Sutekh in Doctor Who's The Legend of Ruby Sunday, a demon-like figure](https://images.immediate.co.uk/production/volatile/sites/3/2024/06/Sutekh-Doctor-Who-d3e911a.png?quality=90&fit=700,467)

Sutekh in Doctor Who's The Legend of Ruby Sunday. BBC

Sutekh is a powerful Osiran and the god of death, first appearing in Doctor Who in 1975 and returning in The Legend of Ruby Sunday (with voice actor Gabriel Woolf reprising his role).

The Doctor defeated Sutekh, AKA the One Who Waits, in Empire of Death by dragging him through the time vortex and undoing all of the deaths he'd caused.

**The Trickster**
-----------------

![Image 8: The Trickster, a hooded figure with an alien face, in The Sarah Jane Adventures](https://images.immediate.co.uk/production/volatile/sites/3/2024/06/Trickster-1838277.png?quality=90&fit=700,467)

The Trickster in The Sarah Jane Adventures. BBC

The Trickster is the main antagonist in Doctor Who spin-off The Sarah Jane Adventures.

While his origins are not entirely known, we do know he's immortal (much like Sutekh) and part of the 'Pantheon of Discord', a group of god-like figures who were banished from the known universe.

The Trickster, also known as the god of traps, makes bargains to change history, feeding on the inevitable chaos that ensues.

**The Mara**
------------

The Mara, previously seen in classic serials Kinda and Snakedance, is the god of beasts.

[![Image 1: 4](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F653fc9cc1fe1c-daniel-bibby.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90)](https://screenrant.com/author/daniel-bibby/) Daniel is a huge sci-fi TV and movie nerd, although his tastes are also quite broad. Contributing to MovieWeb from the UK, Daniel's work can also be found on Screen Rant, Winter is Coming, and Talknerdy.uk. Warning: Spoilers ahead for _Doctor Who_ season 15, episode 2, "Lux."[**_Doctor Who_**](https://screenrant.com/db/tv-show/doctor-who/) season 15, episode 2, "Lux," introduces a villain initially referred to as Mr. Ring-a-Ding, but there is far more to the sentient cartoon character than there appears to be on the surface. That said, the concept of a living animation in the real world is already pretty fascinating, but showrunner **Russell T. Davies finds a way to make Mr. Ring-a-Ding even more compelling**. Not only does Mr. Ring-a-Ding have a connection to [_Doctor Who_'s Pantheon of Gods](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-pantheon-gods-all-10-members/), but he opens the door to one of the biggest fourth wall breaks of [_Doctor Who_'s Disney era](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-1-14-40-disney-confusion/). "Lux" welcomes Alan Cumming to the [_Doctor Who_ season 15 cast](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-15-cast-character-guide/) as the voice of Mr. Ring-a-Ding. It's also the first adventure with Fifteen (Ncuti Gatwa) and Belinda Chandra (Varada Sethu) since the realization at the [end of _Doctor Who_ season 15, episode 1](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-15-episode-1-ending-explained/), "The Robot Revolution," that the TARDIS can't take Belinda home. Their visit to 1952 Miami is part of a larger effort to triangulate the temporal and spatial coordinates that will allow Belinda to return to 2025. However, as is tradition, **the Time Lord and his new companion find more than they bargained for**. Mr. Ring-a-Ding Is Really Lux Imperator, The Pantheon's God Of Light -------------------------------------------------------------------- ### Lux is part of the same group of villains as Sutekh ![Image 2: Lux looking sinister in Doctor Who](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/untitled-48.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2) Although he has the aesthetic appearance of an in-universe cartoon character called Mr. Ring-a-Ding, Cumming's character is really the God of Light, a being named Lux Imperator. Often referred to only as Lux, the God of Light is a member of the same organization as other Pantheon members - like [the Toymaker, the God of Games (Neil Patrick Harris)](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-toymaker-villain-explained-60th-anniversary/), [Maestro, the God of Music (Jinkx Monsoon)](https://screenrant.com/doctor-whos-maestro-villain-identity-powers-explained/), and [Sutekh, the God of Death. (Gabriel Woolf)](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-sutekh-one-who-waits-explained/). > "I am Lux. Lux Imperator, the God of Light! I am the dazzle at the heart of the Pantheon, and the glint in the eyes of the mad. I am the last thing you see before you fall into the abyss." > > Lux in _Doctor Who_ season 15, episode 2, "Lux." Lux is an example of Davies creating an entirely new character to add to the Pantheon, rather than rounding them up from [_Doctor Who_'s classic era](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-classic-era-harsh-realities/) and retconning them into being Gods. Maestro (or arguably Trickster) was the first instance of an original Pantheon God. Appearing only as an animated character, even to those within the world of the show, **Lux is a drastic departure from his _Doctor Who_ predecessors**. Although it initially seems he will be a standalone villain, the return of the musical laugh from "The Giggle" confirms his Pantheon membership in a surprising twist. How Lux Comes To Life & What His Goal Is ---------------------------------------- ### The God of Light enters the story in a moonbeam Before the events of "Lux," Cumming's character had never been mentioned or made an appearance. So, it begs the question of where Lux has been all this time. The "short" answer is that he's been in another universe, and he's only able to arrive in "Lux" after the damage caused to the fabric of reality thanks to David Tennant's Fourteenth Doctor invoking a salt-based superstition at the edge of the universe. So, **Lux has managed to cross over into _Doctor Who_'s primary universe**. However, he doesn't have a corporeal form at first. Because celluloid is purpose-made to capture light, this acts as the perfect bridge for Lux to take form. The moonbeam at the beginning of "Lux" is how the episode's title character enters the fray. After shining through the projection room's skylight and bouncing off the spoon and other reflective objects, **Lux finds his way to an active roll of film being used to show a Mr. Ring-a-Ding cartoon**. Because celluloid is purpose-made to capture light, this acts as the perfect bridge for Lux to take form. The one catch is that he's restricted to images imprinted onto the film, so he duplicates Mr. Ring-a-Ding's physical appearance, which just so happens to be that of a 1950s cartoon. ![Image 3: Custom image of different Doctors in Doctor Who](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/the-first-last-villains-each-doctor-faced-in-doctor-who.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=220&h=182&dpr=2)Related ##### [The First & Last Villains Each Doctor Faced In Doctor Who](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-first-last-villains-list/ "The First & Last Villains Each Doctor Faced In Doctor Who") From the Daleks to the Toymaker, the canonical incarnations of the Doctor all faced incredible Doctor Who villains, but their first and last mattered. **Lux's goal is to bring himself even more into the physical realm by acquiring a body** that would survive away from the movie theater and in the outside world. Because of the footage he's seen in Palazzo, he knows about the various sources of light sitting outside its walls, including nuclear bombs. In his form as the animated Mr. Ring-a-Ding, such immense levels of light would be too much for him to handle, so he aims to fortify himself against the risk. What Lux's Powers Are & How The Doctor Beats Him ------------------------------------------------ ### Light is Lux's number one weapon (& his biggest weakness) Put simply, Lux has the ability to manipulate light. This includes light in the fairly uninteresting sense, like the kind that would come from a lightbulb, but light is almost everywhere. As such, it makes Lux a fearsome villain with incredibly fantastical powers. One of the more fascinating displays of Lux's powers is when he essentially resurrects the late wife of the Palazzo's projectionist, Mr. Reginald Pye. **Lux pulls Mrs Pye from the black-and-white footage owned by her husband and brings her into the physical realm**. Lux's "_Don't make me laugh!_" catchphrase is inherited from the Mr. Ring-a-Ding cartoon. It's not actually Mrs. Pye, but her husband can scarcely tell the physical difference, especially after she gets the technicolor treatment. Lux also has the ability to send characters the other way - from the real world into the realm of light. This is displayed when **Fifteen and Belinda are sent on a journey through Lux's domain**, where they experience life as 2D animated characters, and also meet a group of [_Doctor Who_ fans who have watched all the Time Lord's adventures](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-15-lux-fans-scene-op-ed/) on a TV screen. Formidable though he is, Lux must replicate whatever is happening if a Mr. Ring-a-Ding film is played. This is used against him in "Lux" when Mr. Pye is trying to buy the Doctor and Belinda time to escape. Plus, he can't go outside as Mr. Ring-a-Ding - at least at first. Perhaps most importantly, **Lux can draw out the regeneration energy inside the Doctor**. The God of Light is fascinated by the Time Lord's ability to build himself a new body, which is exactly what Lux is trying to do for himself. After restraining the Doctor, Lux draws the regeneration energy out and absorbs it. As he becomes more three-dimensional, the Doctor grows weaker. Thankfully, Belinda picks up on Fifteen's coded message to destroy the picture house's back wall so that Lux is exposed to direct sunlight. As the Doctor explains, when Belinda is confused, humans are mostly water and can still drown - and the same is true of Lux and light. Although coming into direct contact with sunlight may seem as though it would work to Lux's advantage, it proves too much for him to handle. Instead of growing more powerful, **Lux absorbs more and more of the sun's light**. He grows and grows without end until he leaves Earth's orbit and starts to draw in energy from the light of other celestial bodies and the universe at large. As the Doctor explains, when Belinda is confused, humans are mostly water and can still drown - and the same is true of Lux and light. Is Lux Really Dead At The End Of Doctor Who Season 15, Episode 2? ----------------------------------------------------------------- ### Lux is done for now, but could always come back ![Image 4: Lux floating above the Earth in Doctor Who](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/untitled-49.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2) The implication at the end of "Lux" is that Alan Cumming's _Doctor Who_ character is dead. Interestingly, that doesn't seem to be the case, at least not in the traditional sense. As Belinda points out, **Lux now boasts pretty much all the traits of a God**. He has no physical form, and he's everywhere all at once, as well as also being most things. He becomes at one with the universe, detached from most other desires or concerns. > BELINDA: "So, he's actually a God now. Infinite. Invisible. Intangible." > > THE DOCTOR: "Amen." > > _Doctor Who_ season 15, episode 2, "Lux." Lux doesn't die, but he at least stops being a threat. That being said, there's no reason why he can't return someday. **It doesn't seem likely that a Pantheon God can actually die forever**. The Doctor has managed to defeat several members of the Pantheon so far, but the Toymaker and Sutekh have both come back after their apparent fall in the show's classic era. So, even though Lux Imperator seems to be done for now, his resurgence in **_Doctor Who_**'s future remains a possibility.

Doctor Who – Lux
================

[April 26, 2025](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/2025/04/26/doctor-who-lux/) [Luke Slater](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/author/happyfett/) [1 Comment](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/2025/04/26/doctor-who-lux/#comments)

> “I’m a two-dimensional character, you can’t expect a backstory!”

[![Image 2](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/p0l4g1pb.jpg?w=474)](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/p0l4g1pb.jpg)

…but they sure do hope to get back to 1957 Milwaukee

Dead set on returning to her place of origin, the unreachable May 24th 2025, the Doctor lands the TARDIS the night before and waits a few hours.

Ha! No, you rubes! You clowns!\* He doesn’t do that! He lands down the road and they walk.

Ha again! He doesn’t even try either of those! Instead, he creates a device to triangulate a path based on readings taken at a series of random stops. The first is in 1950s Miami, where a cinema full of people have vanished.

\* This particular line of harranguing will make sense to a small number of readers. For the rest of you, it is an in joke, I neither hate you nor wish to be hated.

Naturally choosing to investigate, the Doctor and Belinda trace the disappearance to Mr Ring-a-Ding, a cartoon character come to life, thanks to the presence of Lux, a god of light who wants to… eat the world, or something. He tries to trap them in the metatext of the cinematic and televisual medium so he can steal the Doctor’s light and become physical, and unless the Doctor can work out his weakness, there’s nothing anyone can do to stop him.

[![Image 3](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/512576-scaled-1.webp?w=474)](https://badmoviemarathon.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/512576-scaled-1.webp)

The Doctor faces another god, and honestly the phrase ‘another god’ seldom makes for a worthwhile antagonist,

So… the Doctor fights another god, and honestly, what’s up with that? It’s been about a year since the Toymaker’s return, we’ve had four out of eleven episodes spent fighting actual gods, and while the Giggle is still a bit creepy, it’s not scary anymore. Three is apparently the limit on the number of gods you can beat before it’s just another day in the TARDIS.

That aside, ‘Lux’ is a decent little episode. My daughter found it engaging and I was entertained. I always appreciate when the show takes the time to remind us that history is not just a fun time, but comes preloaded with racism and other horrors, even before the cartoon space gods arrive. It’s actually a shame that the A plot didn’t play into that aspect more, as it ends up a little anemic by comparison to the never-actually-realised threat of the Doctor being arrested and beaten to death for drinking a cup of coffee while black.

The metatextual moments were fine, and I’m glad the show chose to be kind to its fans. It’s easy to turn that parasocial engagement toxic.

**Story:** 3/5  
**Characters:** 3/5   
**Locals:** 4/5  
**Design:** 4/5

**TOTAL:** 14/20

| | [List of episodes (2005–present)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Doctor_Who_episodes_/(2005%E2%80%93present/) "List of Doctor Who episodes (2005–present)") | "**Silence in the Library**" is the eighth episode of the [fourth series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who_/(series_4/) "Doctor Who (series 4)") of the revived British [science fiction television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction_television "Science fiction television") series _[Doctor Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who "Doctor Who")_. It was first broadcast on [BBC One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_One "BBC One") on 31 May 2008. It is the first of a two-part story; the second part, "[Forest of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_of_the_Dead "Forest of the Dead")", aired on 7 June. The two episodes make up the second two-parter [Steven Moffat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Moffat "Steven Moffat") contributed to the series after "[The Empty Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empty_Child "The Empty Child")" and "[The Doctor Dances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doctor_Dances "The Doctor Dances")" from the [first series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who_/(series_1/) "Doctor Who (series 1)"). It is also the final story that Moffat wrote before replacing [Russell T Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_T_Davies "Russell T Davies") as head writer and showrunner starting from the [fifth series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who_/(series_5/) "Doctor Who (series 5)") in 2010. In the episode, the archaeologist [River Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Song_/(Doctor_Who/) "River Song (Doctor Who)") ([Alex Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Kingston "Alex Kingston")) summons the alien [time traveller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_travel_in_fiction "Time travel in fiction") the [Tenth Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_Doctor "Tenth Doctor") ([David Tennant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tennant "David Tennant")) to a planet-sized [library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library "Library") in the 51st century, where thousands of visitors disappeared without a trace a hundred years earlier when the library was shut off. The episode marks the first appearance of Alex Kingston as River Song, a role she would reprise in the next three series. ”Silence in the Library” was watched by 6.27 million viewers and received highly positive reviews. It was nominated for the [Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation (Short Form)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Award_for_Best_Dramatic_Presentation "Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation"). The [Tenth Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_Doctor "Tenth Doctor") and [Donna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Noble "Donna Noble") land on a planet-sized library in the 51st century simply called the Library. The Doctor has been summoned there, but a scan for life shows the Doctor and Donna as the only humanoid life signs but trillions of nonhuman life forms they cannot see or hear are present. An information node tells the Doctor and Donna that the library sealed itself, but that it has been breached and others are coming. Just then, a team of explorers led by [archaeologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeologist "Archaeologist") [River Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Song_/(Doctor_Who/) "River Song (Doctor Who)") (who sent the message) and financier Strackman Lux, whose grandfather originally built the Library, arrives. The team has come to determine why the library sealed itself 100 years previously. River somehow knows the Doctor, and has a diary with a cover decorated like the [TARDIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TARDIS "TARDIS") with her. She discovers the Doctor has not met her yet in his personal time-line. [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/The_Library.jpg/250px-The_Library.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Library.jpg) The Vashta Nerada inhabiting the suits of the dead explorers, and the information nodes, as shown at the Doctor Who Experience. The Library's operation system appears to be connected to the mind of a young girl living on 21st-century Earth. When the Doctor attempts to access the library computers, the girl causes books to fly from the shelves. The events happening in the library appear to her as television shows. The girl's psychiatrist Dr Moon tells her that the library in her imagination is actually real and that her real world is a lie. He implores her to save the people who have arrived at the library. Lux's secretary Miss Evangelista is attacked by [Vashta Nerada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Doctor_Who_universe_creatures_and_aliens_/(Q%E2%80%93Z/)#Vashta_Nerada "List of Doctor Who universe creatures and aliens (Q–Z)") which strip her flesh clean to the bone instantly. The Doctor and Donna learn that the team are wearing communication devices which can store their thought patterns even after death, and are disturbed to hear Miss Evangelista still talking but acting confused until her pattern degrades. The Doctor explains that the Vashta Nerada are creatures that appear as shadows to hunt but are usually not as aggressive. After noticing the pilot Proper Dave has two shadows, the Doctor and River seal him in his space suit, with the Doctor discovering River has a [sonic screwdriver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_screwdriver "Sonic screwdriver"). The Vashta Nerada still get in, stripping Dave to his bare skeleton. The creatures animate Dave's suit and chase after the others. The Doctor attempts to teleport Donna back to the TARDIS for her safety, but Donna fails to materialise properly. The Doctor finds an information node with Donna's face on it which tells him that Donna has left the library and been saved. Originally, the two-parter was scheduled to take place during the show's [third series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who_/(series_3/) "Doctor Who (series 3)"), with Moffat wanting to introduce the villainous [Weeping Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weeping_Angel "Weeping Angel") in the entry after seeing an angel statue in a graveyard whilst on a family holiday. However, after withdrawing from the writing of series three's first two-part story, Moffat volunteered to write the series' Doctor-lite episode and opted to use the Weeping Angels in what would become "[Blink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink_/(Doctor_Who/) "Blink (Doctor Who)")".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-1) Later, during the fourth series, Moffat revisited his previous ideas. He felt that the library would be a "great setting" for _Doctor Who_ that was not too exotic.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-2) It was the second two-parter Moffat wrote for the show, and the fifth episode in total, after "[The Empty Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empty_Child "The Empty Child")"/"[The Doctor Dances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doctor_Dances "The Doctor Dances"), "[The Girl in the Fireplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Girl_in_the_Fireplace "The Girl in the Fireplace")" and "Blink".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-3) The character of River Song was originally created for the plot to make more sense. Moffat knew that the team of archaeologists would have to trust the Doctor, but that the Doctor's psychic paper could not explain and convince the team why he had appeared in a sealed-off library. Therefore, Moffat intended for the Doctor to know one of the archaeologists. Later, he decided that this idea was too "dull", and instead opted to have one of them know him, but not have the Doctor know her yet (due to mismatched timelines), with hints that we will see and get to know her in future episodes.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-4) A "squareness gun" was used by Song to help the party escape from the Vashta Nerada, just like the sonic blaster [Jack Harkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Harkness "Jack Harkness") ([John Barrowman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Barrowman "John Barrowman")) uses, and which Rose Tyler dubbed with the same name, in the episode "[The Doctor Dances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doctor_Dances "The Doctor Dances")". Moffat stated that it was intended to be the same suggesting it was left in the TARDIS after "[The Parting of the Ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Parting_of_the_Ways "The Parting of the Ways")", and taken by Song in the Doctor's future.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley2008104-5) [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Alex_Kingston_Photo_Op_GalaxyCon_Minneapolis_2019.jpg/250px-Alex_Kingston_Photo_Op_GalaxyCon_Minneapolis_2019.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_Kingston_Photo_Op_GalaxyCon_Minneapolis_2019.jpg) Alex Kingston played the role of [River Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Song_/(Doctor_Who/) "River Song (Doctor Who)"), a mysterious woman from the Doctor's future who he does not know yet. For the role of River Song, whom [executive producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_producer "Executive producer") [Russell T Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_T_Davies "Russell T Davies") described as "sort of the Doctor's wife", the production sought to cast [Kate Winslet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Winslet "Kate Winslet").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-6) One of Winslet's first acting roles was in the [BBC1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_One "BBC One") teen drama _[Dark Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Season "Dark Season")_, written by Davies.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-ten-7) The role of River Song eventually went to [Alex Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Kingston "Alex Kingston"), who had starred in the US drama _[ER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ER_/(TV_series/) "ER (TV series)")_. On Kingston's casting, Davies said "I bloody love her!"[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-daviestimes-8) Kingston had been a fan of _Doctor Who_ as a child.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-TVSquad-9) Kingston was not told her role was supposed to be recurring, learning only later that Moffat always intended for Song to come back for return appearances.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-EW_interview-10) Kingston enjoyed getting to play an unusual [action hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_hero "Action hero") female role, and praised the show for its variety of settings and opportunities "to relive one's childhood fantasies" playing with laser guns and wearing varied costumes from one appearance to the next.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-TVSquad-9) In regards to having to speak complicated dialogue, she said that unlike _ER_, "On _Doctor Who_, I've no idea what some of my lines mean!"[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-radiotimes2-11) Discussing her role alongside Tennant and Tate in her 2008 introductory episode, Kingston said, "We just clicked. I've done guest roles on other shows, but rarely have I felt such a warm bond",[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-radiotimes1-12) a sentiment that Tennant and Tate shared."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-radiotimes2-11) The role of Strackman Lux went to [Steve Pemberton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Pemberton "Steve Pemberton"), who is best known for his work as a member of _[The League of Gentlemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_League_of_Gentlemen "The League of Gentlemen")_. He also appeared in _[Blackpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpool_/(TV_series/) "Blackpool (TV series)")_ with David Tennant.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley200898-13) The roles of the other team members, being minor, went to newcomers, though care was taken to ensure that one could grasp instantly who everyone on the expedition was.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley200898-13) In 2020, Moffat revealed that he had envisioned [Colin Salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Salmon "Colin Salmon")'s character, Dr. Moon, as a future incarnation of the Doctor.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-14) ### Filming and effects \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silence_in_the_Library&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Filming and effects")\] Filming for the two episodes took place in late January and early February 2008, with reshoots taking place in the middle of March.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley200895-15) Filming for the episode consisted of three key locations: [Upper Boat Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Boat_Studios "Upper Boat Studios") for the corridors, walkways and bookcase rooms in the Library, [Brangwyn Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brangwyn_Hall "Brangwyn Hall") for the entrances and under library and [Old Swansea Central Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Swansea_Central_Library "Old Swansea Central Library") as the main set of the library.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley200895-15) The presence of the Vashta Nerada was created with lighting managed by director of photography Rory Taylor. To draw the eye toward the shadows, they were deepened in post-production by visual effects company [The Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mill_/(post-production/) "The Mill (post-production)").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-16) The establishing shots of the CGI cityscape of the Library was created in [Cinema 4D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_4D "Cinema 4D") using the Advanced Render 3 module. This effort was nominated for a [VES Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VES_Award "VES Award") in 2009.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-17) Broadcast and reception ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silence_in_the_Library&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Broadcast and reception")\] Before the episode was aired, _[The Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sun_/(United_Kingdom/) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_ obtained a copy of the script and threatened to release it, to which Moffat responded: "'let them' – I'd like to see _The Sun_ publish that many words in a day!"[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-18) On 16 May, similar to what they did for series 3 in 2007, the BBC announced that to avoid a clash with their coverage of the [Eurovision Song Contest 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_2008 "Eurovision Song Contest 2008"), which took place on 24 May, no _Doctor Who_ episode would air that day, but would instead be pushed back a week to 31 May.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley2008106-19) The week also saw the announcement of Moffat succeeding Davies as showrunner, in a BBC press release on 20 May.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley2008106-19) "Silence in the Library" was scheduled against the final of [ITV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_/(TV_network/) "ITV (TV network)")'s talent contest _[Britain's Got Talent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britain%27s_Got_Talent "Britain's Got Talent")_ and suffered in the ratings as a result. The episode recorded an audience of 6.27 million when adjusted for [time shifting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_shifting "Time shifting"), whereas _Britain's Got Talent_ was viewed by 11.52 million in comparison.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-barb-20) This was the first time since the series' revival in 2005 that _Doctor Who_ did not have the largest audience share in its timeslot. The episode received an [Appreciation Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appreciation_Index "Appreciation Index") score of 89 (considered "Excellent"),[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPixley2008107-21) the joint highest figure the new series had received to date, alongside "The Parting of the Ways", "[Doomsday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomsday_/(Doctor_Who/) "Doomsday (Doctor Who)")" and the following episode "Forest of the Dead". [BBC Three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Three "BBC Three")'s repeat of the episode was watched by 1.35 million viewers, almost double the figures for the equivalent repeat of the previous episode, "[The Unicorn and the Wasp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unicorn_and_the_Wasp "The Unicorn and the Wasp")".[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-barb-20) ### Critical reception and accolades \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silence_in_the_Library&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Critical reception and accolades")\] The episode received positive reviews from critics. Richard Edwards, reviewing for _[SFX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SFX_/(magazine/) "SFX (magazine)")_, gave the episode five out of five stars and called it the "best of the series so far". He particularly praised the fear instilled by the Vashta Nerada and the "intriguing parallel plotline" of the little girl, and highlighted the "chilling and heartbreaking" plot device of the "Data Ghosts".[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-22) Simililarly, Patrick Mulkern of _[Radio Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Times "Radio Times")_ praised the two-parter as a collection of several brilliant ideas, with a backdrop of a child's virtual reality world, and the introduction of a mysterious woman from the Doctor's future.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-23) _[A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.V._Club "A.V. Club")'_s Keith Phipps, giving it an 'A', found the episode "stellar", throwing one big idea after another, against a setting both mysterious and spooky due to the little girl and the Vashta Nerada respectively, ending on a big reveal and a thrilling cliffhanger, making viewers wait a week to unpack what they have seen.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-24) _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")'_s Travis Fickett gave it a rating of 9.2 out of 10, praising the setting of a library with books and "terrifically entertaining dialogue, one mind boggling concept after another, terrific character moments" between all the characters. However, he thought the concept of the Vashta Nerada were "a bit goofy", especially when they took the form of the skeletons.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-25) Ben Rawson-Jones of _[Digital Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Spy "Digital Spy")_ gave "Silence in the Library" four out of five stars, praising the "wonderfully inventive concepts" of the Data Ghosts and Nodes as well as guest stars Kingston, Salmon, and Newton. However, his "slight criticism" was that some aspects were similar to other episodes Moffat had written for _Doctor Who_.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-26) Den of Geek listed the cliffhanger for "Silence in the Library" among the ten greatest of the show in 2011, one which goes beyond menacing into "what is going on" territory for the viewers;[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-27) and _IGN_ named the two-parter one of the best episodes of Tennant's tenure.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-28) This episode, along with "Forest of the Dead", was nominated for a [Hugo Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Award "Hugo Award") in the [Best Dramatic Presentation, Short Form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Award_for_Best_Dramatic_Presentation,_Short_Form "Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation, Short Form") category, but lost out to _[Dr. Horrible's Sing-Along Blog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Horrible%27s_Sing-Along_Blog "Dr. Horrible's Sing-Along Blog")_.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-29) The episode won the 2009 [Constellation Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_Award "Constellation Award") for Best Script in Film or Television.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_note-30) 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_in_the_Library#cite_ref-1)** ["Ask the Execs: Angels and Arrivals"](https://web.archive.org/web/20120826041954/http://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/doctorwho/articles/Ask-the-Execs-Angels-and-Arrivals). 17.content:
_Silence in the Library_ and _Forest of the Dead_ is a two part story from the fourth season of the revival of _Doctor Who_, starring David Tennant and introducing Alex Kingston as River Song.

**Previous Episode:  [_The Doctor’s Daughter_](https://bluetowel.wordpress.com/2012/02/23/doctor-who-the-doctors-daughter-episode-4-6/ "Doctor Who:  The Doctor’s Daughter [Episode 4.6]") • Next Episode: [_Midnight_](https://bluetowel.wordpress.com/2012/09/30/doctor-who-midnight-episode-4-10/ "Doctor Who:  Midnight [Episode 4.10]")**  
_(I know these are not consecutive – more will be filled in as I have the opportunity.)_

**Silence in the Library:**  The Doctor and Donna arrive at the planet-sized Library, to find it completely empty, having been a victim of a mysterious disaster a century prior in which 4000+ people suddenly vanished.  They run into a team of archeologists who are the first to return to the library since then.  The team is organized by the unpleasant Mr. Lux, whose family built the Library, and led by Professor River Song, a mysterious woman who knows the Doctor very closely in his personal future, and even has his future sonic screwdriver.  The Doctor realizes that the Library has become infested with Vashta Narada, a spore-like flesh eating life form that hides in (and resembles) deep shadows.  Members of the archeological team begin to die, although there consciousnesses can remain alive for a short time via special communicators that they use that have a neural link.  The Vashta Nerada animate the space suits of their victims and use them to chase other potential victims around.  Meanwhile, the library seems to be imagined by a little girl who apparently has mental problems.  However, when her dad is not listening, her psychiatrist, Dr. Moon, tells her that the Library is real and that people inside of it are in danger, and that she must save them.  Back in the Libary, the Doctor tries to teleport Donna back to the Tardis for safety, but something goes wrong.  The Doctor discovers that the same fate has befallen her as did the other 4000 inhabitants of the Library just as the animated Vashta Nerada suits start to corner them.

**Forest of the Dead:** The Doctor, River and the other survivors keep on the run while the Doctor tries to find out what happened to Donna.  Donna, meanwhile, finds herself being treated for mental issues by Dr. Moon.  She recovers, gets married to a fellow patient, and has two children before she’s a mysterious woman contacts her and helps her to realize that she is in a simulated environment, where her children are not real.  The woman is Miss Evangelista, the first victim of the Vashta Nerada from the archeological team, whose consciousness has been absorbed by the planet’s computer via the neural relay after she died.  Donna and the other Library inhabitants have been teleported away from danger by the main computer, and are being held within its databank until they can be reactivated safely (ie after the Vashta Nerada are no longer a threat).  The Doctor and the others go to the center of the planet where the main computer core is kept.  There, the Doctor discovers that the computer is actually the little girl – a member of Mr. Lux’s family who was dying.  A virtual world was created for her, with access to all of the books in the universe.   It was she that saved the inhabitants of the Library by teleporting them away, but the strain has begun to overwhelm her.  The Doctor is able to talk down the Vashta Nerada, but the girl / computer begins to self destruct.  The Doctor figures out a way to sacrifice himself to prevent this, but River intervenes and dies in his place.  The Doctor realizes that his future self gave River the sonic screwdriver so that he could secretly place a neural link in her presence, which the Doctor uses to save River by downloading her into the now stable virtual reality environment.

**Comments_:_**  I’ve been amazed to realize lately that there are people out there who don’t like _Silence in the Library_ and its follow-up, which is a fact that I find mystifying.  I think it’s a fantastic two-parter and a highlight of a generally strong fourth season.  The plot is a rich puzzle, manages its different elements very deftly (far more deftly than I was able to describe them in the paragraphs above).  I was engaged and fascinated trying to sort through all that is going on with the Vashta Nerada, the little girl and her therapist, the missing visitors to the library, and of course the introduction or River Song, but it all comes together in a very satisfying way at the end.

There are weaknesses, of course.  The main one is that though the idea of the Vashta Nerada is quite terrifying, they don’t seem very clever, or at least not consistently so.  This vast swarm of micro-organisms (that is at one point shown cruising down a corridor at a good clip, blotting out the lights) that abruptly devours people without warning, decide that most of the time, it’d be in their best interests to lumber around in human space suits for no reason but to give the heroes someone slower to run away from.

Aside from that, and from the slightly cheesy skeletons, it’s great fun.  At the start, one has no idea how to make sense of the scenes with the little girl and Dr. Moon.  That sort of mysterious disconnection is a bit of a highlight of Steven Moffat’s contributions to Doctor Who  as a writer, and I love it.  In the same way that we see in other stories of his, such as _The Empty Child_ and _Blink_, he is able to create what on the surface are completely random (and unsettling) events that seem completely inexplicable, and then peel back the layers until we gain full (or full enough) understanding.

Forest of the Dead is a very good Donna story, allowing her to have her funny moments (“I’ve been dieting!” at her realization that her body is a virtual one) while at the same time pushing the character into new dramatic areas.  Her plight at realizing the truth behind her environment, her world, and especially her children is very chilling and very human.  As a parent myself I can completely sympathize with her inability to just “reject” her children even when she discovers their non-existence.  Catherine Tate’s performance at this, and the aftermath of it all for her, is strong and compelling.

The story, especially _Forest of the Dead_, has some fun with some quite “meta” moments.  Little Charlotte literally watches _Doctor Who_ on television, cowering behind the sofa cushions at the scary moments.  The entire section with Donna in the virtual world has a lot of fun with cinematic language (quite a while before _Inception_ did the same thing).  And the Doctor challenging the Vashta Nerada to “look him up” in all of the books in the Library is sort of like inviting them to watch the entire TV series.

Out of everything, the biggest legacy of the episode is the introduction (and farewell, all in one story) of River Song, entering the scene with her trademark, “Hello, sweetie.”  I’ve heard that she was originally introduced just because it helped the plot if the archeologists would trust the Doctor right away, but that in writing that Moffat decided it’d be more interesting if one of the team members knew the Doctor rather than the other way around.  River is a great character here, lots of fun and full of surprises for the Doctor.  She is also very likeable, which isn’t always the case later on (perhaps it’s a sign of the characters maturity).  Her death at the end of the story is very impacting, and the way she is “saved” is an unexpected triumph.  With the promises that she gives of the Doctor’s future, and the way that the Doctor begins to embrace those promises here, it’s hard to argue that there is any other encounter with a guest character that has ever had such a profound effect on our hero.

The rest of the character work is also good:  Little Charlotte, Donna’s husband Lee, Miss Evangelista, and especially Dr. Moon,  work well.  Colin Salmon, who plays Dr. Moon, especially does a great job, carrying the character’s ambiguity – is a good guy or a bad guy? – very well.  I also like the writing for Mr. Lux – a character we assume is the usual pig-headed bureaucrat we’ve seen on _Doctor Who_ dozens of times, but by the end we discover is actually a man deeply committed to family. The rest of the archeological team are all pretty standard, but that works fine, as it’s their “everyman” quality that makes them sympathetic.

There are lots and lots of great dialogue here…

• When they first arrive, the Doctor describes their location to Donna.

Doctor:  The Library.  So big it doesn’t need a name.  Just a great big “The”.

• A little later, when the Doctor clues in to what’s going on

Doctor:  Ha!  I’m thick!  Look at me, I’m old and thick!  Head’s too full of stuff!  I need a bigger head!

• About the Vashta Nerada, (and reflecting the writer’s ability to take simple things and make them terrifying), the Doctor says

Doctor:  Almost every species in the universe has an irrational fear of the dark, but they’re wrong, because it’s not irrational.  It’s Vashta Nerada.

• A chilling and exciting moment with Dr. Moon and little Charlotte toward the end of Part 1:

Dr. Moon:  Now, listen, this is important.  There’s the real world, and there’s the world of nightmares.  That’s right, isn’t it?  You understand that.  
Charlotte:  Yes, I know, Dr. Moon.  
Dr. Moon:  What I want you to remember is this, and I know it’s hard.  The real world is a lie, and your nightmares are real.  The library is real.  There are people trapped in there, people who need to be saved.  The shadows are moving again.  Those people are depending on you.  Only you can save them.  Only you.

• More on the Vashta Nerada

Doctor:  Normally they live on roadkill, but sometimes people go missing.  Not everyone comes back out of the dark.  
River Song:  Every shadow?  
Doctor:  No.  But any shadow.  
River Song:  So what do we do?  
Doctor:  Daleks – aim for the eyestalk.  Sontarans, back of the neck.  Vashta Nerada – run.  Just run.

• When the Vashta Nerada latch onto Anita…

River Song:  Just keep it together, 0kay?  
Anita:  Keeping it together.  I’m only crying.  I’m about to die, it’s not an overreaction.

and then later

Doctor:  Can I get you anything?  
Anita:  An old age would be nice.  Anything you can do?  
Doctor:  I’m all over it.  
Anita:  Doctor, when we first met you, you didn’t trust Professor Song, and then she whispered a word in your ear, and you did.  My life so far…I could do with a word like that.  What did she say?  _(Pause)_  Give a dead girl a break, your secrets are safe with me.

• Miss Evangelista, distorted inside the virtual world, says insightfully…

Miss Evangelista:  I have the two qualities you require to see absolute truth.  I am brilliant…and unloved.

• The Doctor and River as they talk through his final plan to save the Library…

River Song: What do we do?  
Doctor:  Easy!  We’ll beam all the people out in the data core!  The computer will reset and stop the countdown.  Difficult – Charlotte doesn’t have memory space left to make the transfer.  Easy!  I’ll hook myself up to the computer, she can borrow my memory space!  
River Song:  Difficult!  It’ll kill you stone dead!  
Doctor:  Yeahh, it’s easy to criticize.  
River Song:  You’ll burn out both your hearts and don’t think you’ll regenerate!  
Doctor:  I’ll try my hardest not to die, honestly, it’s my main thing.  
River Song:  Doctor–!  
Doctor:  I’m right! This will work.  Shut up!  Now listen, you and Lux, you’re going back up to the main library, try to empty any other data cells you can find for maximum download, and before you say anything else, Professor, can I just mention in passing as you’re here, shut up!  
River Song:  Hh!  I hate you sometimes!  
Doctor:  I know!

• The Doctor scares off the Vashta Nerada (it’s lucky for him that they know how to read).

Doctor:  Don’t play games with me!  You just killed someone I liked, that is not a safe place to stand!  I’m the Doctor and you’re in the biggest library in the universe.  Look me up.

• The farewell scene between the Doctor and River is very moving, with David Tennant and especially Alex Kingston doing an excellent job.

Doctor:  Oh, no no no no, come on, what are you doing?  That’s my job.  
River Song:  Oh and I’m not allowed to have a career, I suppose?  
Doctor:  Why am I handcuff–why do you even have handcuffs?  
River Song:  Spoilers.

and a moment later

River:  Funny thing is, this means you’ve always known how I was going to die.  All the time we’ve been together, you knew I was coming here.  The last time I saw you – the real  you, the future you, I mean – you turned up on my doorstep with a new haircut and a suit.  You took me to Deryllium, to see the Singing Towers.  What a night that was.  The Towers sang, and you cried.  You wouldn’t tell me why, but I suppose you knew it was time, my time.  Time to come to the library.  You even gave me your screwdriver, that should have been a clue.  There’s nothing you can do.  
Doctor:  You can let me do this!  
River:  If you die here it’ll mean I’ve never met you.  
Doctor:  Time can be rewritten!  
River:  Not those times!  Not one line, don’t you dare!  It’s okay, it’s okay, it’s not over for you.  You’ll see me again.  You and me.  Time and space.  You watch us run.  
Doctor:  River, you know my name.  You whispered my name in my ear.  There’s only reason I would ever tell anyone my name.  There’s only one time I could.  
River:  Hush now.  Spoilers.

• Afterwards, as Donna and the Doctor reconnect over what has happened…

Donna:  I made up the perfect man.  Gorgeous, adores me, and hardly ever speak a word.  what does that say about me?  
Doctor:  Everything.  Sorry, did I say “everything”?  I meant to say “nothing”.  I was aiming at “nothing”.  I accidentally said “everything”.  
Donna:  What about you?  You all right?  
Doctor:  I’m always all right.  
Donna:  Is all right special Time-Lord code for “really not all right at all”?  
Doctor:  Why?  
Donna:  Because I’m all right too.

• This is the first episode of _Doctor Who_ that I know of that ends with a voice over / poem.  In this case, it starts just as the Doctor comes to realization that River can be saved.

River Song (voice over):  When you run with the Doctor, it feels like it will never end, but however hard you try, you can’t run forever.  Everybody knows that everybody dies, and nobody knows it like the Doctor.  But I do think that all the skies of all the worlds might just turn dark if he ever, for one moment, accepts it.

and then, as the Doctor begins to embrace his future and opens the Tardis the snap of his fingers…

River Song (voice over):  Somedays are special.  Somedays are so, so blessed.  Somedays nobody dies at all.  Now and then, every once in a very long while, every day in a million days when the wind stands fair and the Doctor comes to call, everybody lives.

**Things to watch out for:**

I love Steven Moffat, but he does enjoy using the a lot of similar ideas in his stories.  The Doctor’s scaring off the Vashta Nerada foreshadows something very similar that happens in _The Eleventh Hour_.  The Vashta Nerada using the remnant of their victim’s consciousnesses to communicate is something the Weeping Angels do in a different way in _Time of Angels_.  The “squareness gun” that River uses is just like the sonic blaster used by Jack Harkness in _The Doctor Dances_ (actually, if the internet is to be believed, Moffat’s speculates it may be the same gun, picked up from the Tardis by River in the future).  There also references to how things are different in the 51st Century, “Spoilers”, the Crash of the Byzantium (from _The Time of Angels_), “Everybody lives,” and others that appear elsewhere in the series in the past and the future.

Also, this wasn’t a Moffat episode, but the “ghosting” with Miss Evangelista is similar to what happens with Astrid Peth in _Voyage of the Damned_.

River says, “I lied.  I’m always lying,” which is something that become very true and very important to the character in the future.

When River realizes that the Doctor doesn’t know who she is, it’s a devastating and painful moment for her, that she anticipates in conversation in Season Six’s _The Impossible Astronaut_.

There are pictures on the wall in Charlotte’s home of a blond girl and a wolf that may be a reference to Rose Tyler and Bad Wolf.

**Making sense of it all (Warning:  blatant spoilers for the rest of the series)**:

I don’t know if Moffat had any indication that he would be taking over as the show’s lead producer in a couple of years after this story, but either way he did an excellent job here in setting up River’s relationship with the Doctor, and also foreshadowing the kind of man the Doctor will become under Moffat’s tenure as showrunner.  River says this about the Doctor to Anita:

River Song:  Yes, the Doctor is here.  He came when I called, just like he always does.  But not _my_ Doctor.  Now my Doctor, I’ve seen whole armies turn and run away, and he’d just swagger off back to his Tardis and open the doors with a snap of his fingers.  The Doctor in the Tardis, next stop everywhere.

Basically, River’s appearance here comes after all the other ones that have ever been aired.  Presumably, she earned her pardon after the crash of the Byzantium and is no longer imprisoned, allowing her to “make professor” and be part of this expedition.  (Actually, I just read online somewhere that River is still in the authority’s custody in this story, but I don’t see any indication of that in the story – in fact she starts to say she’s with a particular university).  River recognizes the Doctor in his 10th incarnation but doesn’t know that he couldn’t have experienced the crash of the Byzantium yet, so she isn’t fully aware of what order his incarnations come in.  A lot of other stories suggest that the Doctor and River basically meet in “reverse” order, but the fact that she doesn’t seem to know what order his regenerations come in would seem to indicate that their encounters are a bit more random.   Indeed, her appearance in the mini-episode Last Night would seem to confirm this.

**Last Word:**   Dramatic.  Funny.  Frightening.  Mysterious.  Tragic.  Triumphant.  It’s hard to pick.  But more than any other episode of the Russell T. Davies-era of Doctor Who, this one serves as a pilot of sorts to what’s to come when Steven Moffat takes the reins a year later.

**Previous Episode:  [_The Doctor’s Daughter_](https://bluetowel.wordpress.com/2012/02/23/doctor-who-the-doctors-daughter-episode-4-6/ "Doctor Who:  The Doctor’s Daughter [Episode 4.6]") • Next Episode: [_Midnight_](https://bluetowel.wordpress.com/2012/09/30/doctor-who-midnight-episode-4-10/ "Doctor Who:  Midnight [Episode 4.10]")**  
_(I know these are not consecutive – more will be filled in as I have the opportunity.)_
